items.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
items.summary:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the op
items.text:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hitthe Kerch bridge - a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic sea port of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

items.summary:
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Search and rescue operations are racing against time in Nigeria after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesper
items.text:
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Search and rescue operations are racing against time in Nigeria after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.
The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.
Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.
The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.
Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.
"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.
"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.
- Why do Nigeria's boat disaster keep happening? 
  - Published20 July
Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.
"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.
The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.
"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.
In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.
He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.
Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.
In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to a
items.text:
Nigeria’s President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water – failures that plague ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues..
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: “On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won’t know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
“The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the 16 January election.
Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

items.text:

Former Icelandic PM says world’s great powers are flexing their muscles
Iceland’s former prime minister warns climate change remains an existential threat as global power politics sidelines action.
Iceland’s former prime minister says that although climate change has fallen lower down on the international political agenda, it remains an existential crisis.
Katrin Jakobsdottir says our warming world is not just a catastrophe for nature, but a health and security emergency that cannot be ignored.
Her country is on the front lines of that emergency, with the Arctic warming at four times the rate of the rest of the world.
Almost all of Iceland’s glaciers are rapidly retreating – one was declared “dead” in 2019.
Jakobsdottir says it all comes at a time when the world’s biggest powers are flexing their muscles – and the politics of compromise are being squeezed out.

items.title: Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show
items.summary:
Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.
Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the le
items.text:
Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.
Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. They outline a plan, produced days before July’s final of the 2026 World Cup, to profit from the sport’s burgeoning commercial revenues for almost a century.
Infantino hopes to be re-elected for a fourth term as president in March and is the favourite to win that contest.
An internal Fifa risk assessment dated 17 July, designed as one of the final steps before concluding the FFE agreement, spells out the scheme’s extraordinary scope. “This deal provides for Fifa to create a for-profit subsidiary which would have all the commercial rights for Fifa events transferred to it for commercial exploitation for the next 96 years,” one section reads.
Another internal Fifa document written the following day, outlining the proposed agreement with Thrive, says the deal’s contract period “would be for rolling 12-year license periods to a sum maximum total of 96 years” and goes further in stating Fifa would assume 51% ownership “in perpetuity”.
The existence of a lucrative “management incentive plan” for unnamed individuals helming the scheme casts into stark light the extent to which its architects could have profited. The plan is first mentioned in a term sheet and “backstop letter” drawn up by Thrive on 17 July, which refers to FFE as “Project Box”, and sets aside up to 5% of FFE’s stock as a bonus pool for the new firm’s management. In theory it could have paid out up to $50m (£38.2m) for each $1bn added to the scheme’s value above $20bn, which was its initial valuation.
The term sheet says the plan “will permit the issuance of profits interests representing up to 5% of the fully diluted capitalisation of FFE, which will dilute all unitholders on a pro rata basis”. According to the Fifa memo the pool’s existence aimed to “ensure sufficient motivation to perform well”.
A further clause states that, if Fifa breached its agreement with Thrive or completed an agreement with a rival party, Thrive would have been entitled to a break fee totalling 1.25% – $250m – of FFE’s worth. Fifa would not have been permitted to engage in talks with other potential lead buyers for a year, or until the FFE deal closed.
Fifa’s memo of 18 July confirms there was no tender process “owing to the specific and unique nature of the proposed investment”. The risk assessment document confirms its own finance department was “not directly privy to the terms of the transaction”, casting further doubt about the processes followed in pursuing the deal.
Fifa declined to comment when contacted by the Guardian. The world governing body has consistently denied that Infantino stood to profit personally from FFE, which will raise questions as to who would have benefited from the management incentive plan.
The documents make clear that the issuance of so-called MIP units would be managed by the board of FFE, which Infantino was due to chair.

items.summary:
Flights grounded in Belgium due to strike against austerity measures
- Published
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in t
items.text:
Flights grounded in Belgium due to strike against austerity measures
- Published
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

items.title: COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
items.summary:
COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in blow to climate agenda.
United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding
items.text:
COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
UN member states fail to agree on how to fast-track action to reverse global warming in blow to climate agenda.
United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.
Known as COP31, the conference in Antalya, Turkiye, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.
The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia.
It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark, which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.
So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?
Why did COP31 collapse?
The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.
Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture, the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.
Cosima Cassel, programme lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.
The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the main driver of global warming.
The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after some 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.
On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.
“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”
Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.
Sebastien Duyck, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.
“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”
What’s next for the UN process – and for the planet?
The collapse of the climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.
The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.
Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.
“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.
However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.
“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.
Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.
Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.
The UN Environment Programme last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.

items.title: WSL talking points: Captain Spence inspires Spurs shock win at City and Lionesses impress
items.summary: Drew Spence rolled back the years with a vintage performance as her Tottenham side produced a shock 3-1 victory away against the defending champions, Manchester City. The 34-year-old marshalled the midfield and then had the vision to thread an outstanding through ball that split the City defence and
items.text:
Drew Spence rolled back the years with a vintage performance as her Tottenham side produced a shock 3-1 victory away against the defending champions, Manchester City. The 34-year-old marshalled the midfield and then had the vision to thread an outstanding through ball that split the City defence and found the run of Matilda Vinberg, who put Spurs 2-1 up. “She’s unbelievable. There are so many more gears in Drew and I wish I’d been able to work with her a bit earlier [in my career] because her leadership is second to none,” the Tottenham head coach, Martin Ho, said of the club captain. “Her performance levels, since I’ve been here, week on week have grown. She is covering every blade of grass and leads by example. For me, she’s one of the best midfielders in the league.” Tom Garry
London City Lionesses head into the international break with a spring in their step, their 6-2 defeat of Crystal Palace helping them to move to within two points of City and four of league leaders Chelsea, who both dropped points at the weekend. There was a resilience to Eder Maestre’s team in their last game before the international break and the full impact of their squad depth was on show against Palace. The visitors cancelled out Daniëlle van de Donk’s opener and pulled a goal back to make it 3-2 after 64 minutes but they ultimately could not cope with the fresh legs London City could turn to in the second half. Talk may be focused on the big-spending side being in the running for Champions League football next season, but on the basis of recent form, and with Chelsea up next in mid December, thoughts may turn to am unlikely title challenge. SW
After 10 straight defeats in the WSL, Charlton finally have something to show for their efforts, registering their first point of the season on Sunday. It has been a tough few months for the promoted side who have been statistically interesting for all the wrong reasons. In their 1-1 draw with Aston Villa, it was their bravery and work rate that shone through as they set about defending a 17th-minute lead. They had to spend significant periods without the ball but kept Villa to eight shots and matched their three on target. At the heart of it was the 21-year-old Keira Flannery who led the midfield with a performance that was beyond her years. She exemplified the character on show in stepping up to take Charlton’s early penalty despite having missed from the spot a fortnight previous. “I’m so proud of the girls,” she said. “We all dug deep and stuck it out to the end. A point is massive. It’s a stepping stone.” Sophie Downey
“You’re nothing special, we draw every week,” sang the Emirates faithful as an abject Arsenal were held to yet another stalemate by West Ham, becoming the first team in WSL history to draw their first six home games. This was probably the poorest performance of their disappointing season, the home side generating an xG of just 0.88. By half-time, they had registered one shot on target and failed to get out of their stupor until the final quarter. The full-time boos were reflected by high emotions on the pitch as the pressure on head coach, Renée Slegers, continues to mount. “I take my responsibilities because the results haven’t been good enough,” she said. “We’re not creating good enough chances to the final third, from all phases. It’s not the Arsenal standard and we need to do that better.” One positive of the afternoon was the news that Lisa Baum was stable after being carried off on a stretcher in the first half. The club confirmed that she was responding well having suffered from “shortness of breath”. SD
Chelsea had 47 touches in the Liverpool box and 19 shots but came away from St Helens with a scoreless draw. The Blues have scored just three goals in their last five games in all competitions, having found the net 30 times in the 11 matches prior to that. The goals have dried up. Getting their attack clicking without the injured duo of Melvine Malard and Lauren James will be critical if they are to find the balance between attack and defence that Sonia Bompastor says they need. “I’m really happy with a lot of things we are doing right now. When you have ambitions, when you want to win titles, you need to make sure to find the right balance between being strong defensively but also being able to score goals,” she said. Their defence is doing the heavy lifting, with the fewest goals conceded in the WSL – five, with Arsenal and Everton next best with 11 conceded – and none in Europe, and they need their attack to share the load. Suzanne Wrack
Failing to defend a set-piece cost Birmingham badly for the second week in a row as they conceded a 94th-minute winner against Manchester United, undoing much of the promoted side’s good work in a close contest. Second-from-bottom Birmingham, who were beaten 1-0 after conceding from a back-post header from a free-kick last time out away at Aston Villa, were again caught out with a far-post delivery, this time with Simi Awujo nodding in to give Manchester United victory. Eva Olid’s visitors are now unbeaten in nine WSL matches, winning six of those, and are enjoying a club-record 14-match unbeaten streak in all competitions, while Birmingham have lost four WSL games on the bounce. TG
Scott Phelan said Everton need to be more consistent in attack after their 1-0 defeat to Brighton. Phelan’s side have scored just eight goals in 11 league games this season – only 14th-placed Charlton have scored fewer. Everton had 12 shots on goal in the game, six of which were blocked. The result leaves them 11th in the league and they will have to find their shooting boots soon to avoid falling down further, especially with fixtures against Arsenal and Manchester City coming before the Christmas break. “We’ve been OK defensively,” Phelan said. “Those attacking phases of play need to be more consistent. items.title: Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
items.summary:

Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
A series of drone strikes on Russian vessels in Libyan and Finnish territories fuels fears that the war in Ukraine is spreading.
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship and striking a cargo vessel off Libya’s coast, raising concerns about the Russia-Ukraine war widening geographically.
“It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Monday.
The attack targeted the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo vessel MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said was used to transport weapons.
The attacks come amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian naval assets, energy infrastructure and vessels linked to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions.
The developments have also raised questions about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, and the risk of drawing other nations into the conflict, nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Here is what we know about the attacks, who may be behind them and what they mean for the expanding reach of the war.
What do we know about the attacks?
The Russian Navy’s Merkury was struck at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, triggering an explosion and fire.
Satellite imagery showed most of the corvette had capsized and sunk, with only its bow visible above water.
Zelenskyy confirmed the sinking on Monday, saying a Russian Kamov Ka-27 military helicopter was also destroyed.
“Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit,” he added.
A day earlier, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew members were evacuated, with one slightly injured.
In Finland, the military assessed the vessel was likely struck by Ukraine. Russian authorities said two drones hit the Sparta II in international waters. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack.
Zelenskyy said his country would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas in response to Russia’s aggression.
Kyiv’s attacks come as Russia has intensified its air attacks across Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, drones and guided bombs. Energy facilities, bridges, Black Sea ports and other civilian infrastructure have been targeted in Ukraine, which has countered with attacks on Russian energy sites and other targets.
What have Libya and Russia said?
Libya’s eastern administration condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and said it had requested an international investigation through the United Nations.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
Saddam Haftar, son of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, said Libya’s security and sovereignty are a “national responsibility that cannot tolerate political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to promote accusations and stir up fears”.
“Rather, it requires prioritising the national interest and dealing responsibly with everything that affects our country’s security and stability,” he said in a statement on Facebook.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli also commented on the incident, saying it was concerned by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
Meanwhile, the UN has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.
On Monday, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote in a post on X.
The oil-rich nation has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
In September, Libya denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the northwest of the country to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The origin of Sunday’s attack is still not confirmed.
How many Russian vessels have been attacked in recent weeks?
At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, including the Merkury, MV Angara and Sparta II.
The Finnish military also reported detecting a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland during Ukrainian drone attacks the previous week.
In March, a Russian LNG tanker sank off Libya’s coast following an attack Moscow blamed on Ukraine.
In December 2025, Ukraine claimed responsibility for striking a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.
Is the Ukraine-Russia war expanding geographically?
Academic Alexey D Muraviev says the conflict has already expanded beyond Ukraine.
“The Mediterranean has firmly become an external theatre of operations, particularly maritime operations,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
He said the vessels targeted in Libyan and Finnish territories were likely involved in transporting military equipment or other supplies to Africa, potentially supporting Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates alongside Moscow-aligned governments.
Muraviev said Ukrainian forces had previously confronted Russian security personnel in Africa, demonstrating that the conflict had already extended beyond its original battlefield.
“Even in this sense, there have been cases when the war in Ukraine effectively extended onto the African continent,” he said.

items.text:
German police respond to multiple school bomb threats
November 23, 2026
Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.
They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.
More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.
What did police say about the bomb threats?
Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.
"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages."
Police said they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.
"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.
Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.
Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.
As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."
Various disruptive incidents targeting Europe in recent weeks
This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Europe.
It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.
This is a developing story, more to follow...

items.title: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
items.summary:
The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.
Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for
items.text:
The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.
Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.
Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.
The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.
Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.
Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.
Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.
Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.
But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said.
The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”.
“Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune.
Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.
Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program.
The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.
An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency.
Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.
A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped.

items.title: Inside Fifa and US Soccer’s plan for 2031 World Cup: ‘the largest women’s sporting event in history’
items.summary: The biggest and most lucrative event in the history of women’s sport will be confirmed at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress in Zurich on Monday, with a joint bid from the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031’s Women’s World Cup to be formally ratified by a vote of Fifa’s 211 m
items.text:
The biggest and most lucrative event in the history of women’s sport will be confirmed at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress in Zurich on Monday, with a joint bid from the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031’s Women’s World Cup to be formally ratified by a vote of Fifa’s 211 member associations.
In the bid book submitted to Fifa last year the prospective hosts pledged to generate total revenues of $4bn if awarded hosting rights, which would represent a staggering increase on the $570m earnings from the last World Cup held in Australia and New Zealand three years ago, the first women’s tournament to break even.
While Fifa is forecasting an almost doubling of tournament revenues to $1bn for next year’s competition in Brazil, achieving a further fourfold growth by 2031 would appear to be challenging.
The United Kingdom’s bid for the 2035 tournament, which will also be ratified on Monday, does not include a revenue target. So how do the US and their co-hosts plan to generate $4bn, and what will be the impact on fans?
The legacy of 2026
Fifa has yet to publish its financial accounts relating to last summer’s men’s World Cup, but it was undoubtedly a huge success. Gianni Infantino told the national associations on the eve of the final in New Jersey last July that Fifa’s revenue projection for the 2023-2026 cycle had increased from $11bn to $15bn, the majority of which was the product of the World Cup itself.
Emboldened by that success, the US Soccer Federation is confident $4bn is a realistic target for 2031, a projection largely based on bringing in $1.4bn from commercial deals, $1.25bn in matchday revenue and $1bn in broadcast income.
“It is a very significant increase from 2023, but I expect [the] 2027 [Women’s World Cup] to continue to be a step forward, and in 2031 to really blow this out of the park because of the maturity of our market here and the excitement that we see,” Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy who will present the bid to Fifa in Zurich, told the Guardian.
“The market here in the US is unlike anywhere else. The 2026 World Cup will be well north of $10bn in revenue, and we’re looking at a tournament with the same number of teams involved. We do have a high level of confidence in that revenue number. We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history.”
Stadiums
The most likely driver of growth is the sheer size of the would-be hosts’ plans for the tournament, which will be the first women’s World Cup to feature 48 teams, increasing the number of matches from 64 to 104.
Just as significantly, most games will be played at large NFL stadiums, with the 13 of the provisional shortlist of 20 venues in the official bid – 14 in the US, four in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica – having capacities of more than 60,000.
To further illustrate the scale of the tournament’s ambitions, seven of these US-based stadiums hosted matches at the 2026 World Cup, with three others having staged games at the 2025 Fifa Club World Cup.
While some smaller stadiums will be used in the group stages, the hosts are targeting a total 4.5 million tickets sold, which would bring average crowds of 43,000 per match, enough to generate ticket revenue of $550m, more than 10 times the $43m made from ticket sales of 1.8 million in 2023.
The bid also projects hospitality sales of $300m, plus $400m in other match day income such as merchandising, parking and transport.
The bid actually contains 50 potential stadiums across 35 different cities, and the initial shortlist is largely theoretical at this stage, with the final decision on venues to be taken by Fifa by the end of 2028.
All of the US venues are in operation other than the proposed redevelopment of the Washington Commanders’ RFK Stadium, which is due to be completed in 2030 but is under consideration.
Mercedes-Benz Stadium (Atlanta), AT&T Stadium (Dallas), SoFi Stadium (Los Angeles) and MetLife Stadium (New Jersey) have been identified as the most likely candidates to host the final, although that decision will not be taken until 2030.
“We think every knockout round can be in a 60,000-plus seat stadium,” Cosler said. “We’ve got the infrastructure to do that, and I have a high level of confidence that every knockout round game can be a sellout. The success of our women’s national team and the NWSL has proven that we’ve got the demand for that.”
Ticket prices
Fifa’s Evaluation Report published earlier this month is even more bullish than the bid in terms of the potential value of ticket sales, claiming that the widespread use of NFL stadiums should mean that ticketing and hospitality revenues “significantly exceed” the $550m forecast, which is described as “a very conservative position with significant upside potential”.
Given that the bid is forecasting a tenfold increase in revenue from the 2023 tournament based on selling two-and-a-half times more tickets, it is clear that the prices will also increase significantly from that tournament. However, lead bidders US Soccer are determined to make the event more accessible than last summer’s men’s World Cup.
“We propose a pricing table that balances what the women deserve in terms of the revenue generated from this tournament, but also access in a way that will continue to grow the game,” Cosler said. “I think there are some really good initiatives that US Soccer has done with our own national team games. We’ve partnered with local universities. We’ve offered $25 tickets that have resulted in filling stadiums and success. This isn’t a charity, but at the same time, we want this game to be accessible to fandom everywhere.”
In comparison to the men’s World Cup and other premium events in the US the pricing structure proposed in the bid looks affordable, with tickets ranging from $35 to $120 in the group stage, and $120 to $600 for the final.

items.text:
Walmart will let Meta’s Muse shop on its website on your behalf, allowing the AI agent to find and purchase Black Friday deals. Tomorrow, on Tuesday November 24th, the retail giant will roll out a live implementation of the Agent Gateway it announced last month, which helps AI agents find relevant products for you without sharing your purchase history, according to Walmart.
Meta Muse can do your Black Friday shopping at Walmart
The Walmart Agent Gateway is about to launch with Muse support, with other apps and agents ‘on the way.’
Muse can make purchases through Walmart’s “Agent Profiles,” which provide a dedicated space for agent activity within your Walmart customer account. These profiles also allow you to set spending limits, approve purchases, and check the purchase history of everything bought by Muse. While other online retailers like Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents from browsing their platforms, Walmart says that support for Meta’s Muse is “just the beginning,” and that additional Walmart shopping experiences for other AI agents and apps are “on the way.”
Here are Walmart’s instructions for shopping its website via Muse:
1. Tell Muse what you need. For example, ask it to find a great TV deal or show you which Walmart Black Friday deals are available for delivery. Muse can help you explore products and build your basket.
2. Set your shopping rules. Muse will take you to Walmart to sign in, then bring you back to Muse. The first time you add an item to your cart, you’ll set up your Agent Profile on Walmart within your Walmart account, including a spending limit you’re comfortable with.
3. Check out. Complete your purchase within the conversation using a card saved in your Walmart account, with the same Walmart prices you’d find on Walmart.com. And if something isn’t quite right, Walmart’s return policy still applies.
Update, November 23rd: Walmart informed The Verge after publication that the Agent Gateway launch has been delayed by 24 hours. The ability to shop on Walmart via Muse will now be available on November 24th.

items.text:
AI dispute divides Germany's dubbing industry
November 23, 2026
When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.
For over 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.
The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.
But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.
Netflix contract sparks AI dispute
Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.
The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.
They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.
"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."
"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.
Union says deal offers legal safeguards
The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.
Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.
Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.
If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.
"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.
Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.
"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."
He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.
Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.
"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.
Voice actor plans legal challenge
Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon character Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.
"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."
He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.
According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.
The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.
For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"
Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.
Industry fears growing AI impact
For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.
Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.
"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.
Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.
"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.
But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."
Edited by: Tim Rooks

items.text:
CAS decision on Senegal’s AFCON 2025 title appeal on Tuesday
Senegal are contesting CAF’s decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal winning the final 1-0 in January.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) will release its decision on Senegal’s appeal against being stripped of this year’s Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title on Tuesday.
Senegal are contesting the decision of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal beating the hosts 1-0 in extra time in January’s final in Rabat, and the outcome will be announced on Tuesday, the court confirmed on Monday.
It did not give a time for the announcement.
CAS heard the arguments of Senegal, Morocco and CAF in Lausanne in early October.
It had initially promised a decision within days of the hearing on October 8 but then decided to issue a complete ruling, including legal grounds, known as a CAS Award. That process requires several weeks.
CAS Awards hold the same value as a national court judgement, enforceable in accordance with the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. Awards may be enforced by sports federations or state courts, depending on the circumstances.
In the final, Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play.
Morocco missed the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory.
However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to Morocco.
Senegal appealed the CAF ruling to sport’s highest court, CAS, on March 25, but it was heard some six months later. The basis of its arguments is that the referee’s decision is final and he allowed the match to be completed.
The CAS panel is presided over by French sports law expert Gerald Simon, with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based lawyer and professor of law at the University of Zurich, Ulrich Haas.

items.text:
Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism
November 23, 2026
Initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts toward the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.
The"Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.
The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.
Numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat. "In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.
Lasting damage to democracy in Germany?
According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.
The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany. The in parts far-right extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Amadeu Antonio Foundation board member Tahera Ameer.
The promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.
During the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need new areas of focus," he said. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, according to him.
But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS), the nationwideOFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims, CLAIM.
The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.
AfD: 'Program to secure power by the Left'
The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself."
If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.
In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.
A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available."
However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.
How is democratic civil society prioritized?
"Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are currently not seeing. And that is very unsettling."
Many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color. "The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered, if someone needs support."
For organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Lina Mitschke lamented.
The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.
This article was originally written in German.

items.title: PLO Lumumba renews push for EACC prosecutorial powers to strengthen graft fight
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – Renowned legal scholar Prof Patrick Lumumba has renewed calls for the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) to be granted prosecutorial powers, arguing that the agency’s dependence on other institutions to prosecute corruption cases undermines the effectiveness of the
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – Renowned legal scholar Prof Patrick Lumumba has renewed calls for the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) to be granted prosecutorial powers, arguing that the agency’s dependence on other institutions to prosecute corruption cases undermines the effectiveness of the war against graft.
Lumumba said the decision to deny the anti-graft agency independent prosecutorial authority was deliberate, warning that the existing arrangement leaves investigators frustrated when cases they have painstakingly built encounter delays or setbacks at the prosecution stage.
He argued that allowing EACC to investigate and prosecute cases would give it greater ownership of investigations and improve the chances of successfully pursuing corruption suspects, particularly within the political class.
“People don’t want an EACC with very sharp teeth. They want an EACC that can bite and is frustrated. They will not tell you, but I’m telling you on their behalf,” Lumumba said.
Speaking during a two-day workshop for media practitioners on integrity in leadership and elections at Whitesands Beach Resort in Mombasa, the scholar recalled discussions held during the constitutional review process in which he advocated for the commission to have prosecutorial powers.
Lumumba said he and the then chairperson of the Kenya Anti-Corruption Commission had pushed for the powers during a meeting chaired by the then Prime Minister, but their proposal faced resistance from senior government officials.
He recounted that members of the working committee opposed the proposal, arguing that an empowered anti-corruption agency would become too powerful.
“They said, ‘We will make EACC a monster. We cannot allow them’,” he recalled.
Lumumba said the decision to retain a separation between investigations and prosecutions had left the commission reliant on other institutions, recalling instances when investigation files submitted to the then Attorney General were returned for further investigations.
He argued that prosecutors who take over cases at the final stage may lack the same depth of understanding and enthusiasm as investigators who have followed the evidence from the beginning.
“I can’t agree with you more, and I think it is something that when we are serious about fighting corruption, particularly the political class, give the power to prosecute and finality in some of the decisions,” he said while responding to a question posed by a journalist.
His remarks revive a longstanding debate over whether Kenya’s anti-corruption framework gives EACC sufficient authority to translate investigations into successful prosecutions.
The call comes as the country prepares for the 2027 General Election, with integrity and accountability emerging as key concerns in the vetting of political aspirants.
EACC Commissioner Col. (Rtd) Alfred Mshimba said the commission submitted integrity records of 241 individuals for consideration during the 2022 General Election, but only five were disqualified.
He questioned whether institutions were doing enough to ensure that constitutional standards on integrity and ethical leadership were enforced when Kenyans elect their leaders.
“These experiences raise an important question: Are we doing enough, as institutions and as a country, to ensure that integrity is given the attention it deserves when electing our leaders?” Mshimba posed.
He said some individuals flagged during the 2017 electoral process were subsequently arrested, charged and convicted of corruption-related offences, while others were removed from office through impeachment proceedings over violations relating to Chapter Six of the Constitution.
In a separate address delivered on his behalf by EACC Director of Investigations Paschal Mweu, Chief Executive Officer Abdi A. Mohamud said the commission would intensify integrity verification of individuals seeking elective positions ahead of the 2027 polls.
Mohamud clarified that EACC does not have the constitutional mandate to independently bar candidates from contesting elections, noting that the responsibility rests with the IEBC.
He said the commission investigates integrity concerns and submits findings and recommendations to the electoral body based on constitutional requirements and agreed verification criteria.
The CEO disclosed that EACC receives more than 20,000 self-declaration forms from individuals seeking nomination as candidates during election years.
The commission has also investigated 228 allegations involving forged academic and professional certificates, recommending prosecution in 134 files forwarded to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.
Of those cases, 60 are pending before courts, while 50 have been concluded, resulting in 45 convictions and five acquittals.
EACC has also recovered Sh41.2 million acquired through the use of forged academic and professional qualifications.
Mohamud said the commission would continue examining documents submitted alongside self-declaration forms to prevent falsified certificates from being used to secure clearance for elective positions.

items.title: Ruto Defends Nzoia Sugar Leasing Deal, Says Factory Remains Bungoma Property
items.summary:
BUNGOMA, Kenya, Nov 23 – President William Ruto has hailed the leasing of Nzoia Sugar Company to private investor Rai Group, describing the miller’s turnaround as historic following improvements in production, profitability and payments to sugarcane farmers.
Ruto said the company, which was on the b
items.text:
BUNGOMA, Kenya, Nov 23 – President William Ruto has hailed the leasing of Nzoia Sugar Company to private investor Rai Group, describing the miller’s turnaround as historic following improvements in production, profitability and payments to sugarcane farmers.
Ruto said the company, which was on the brink of collapse three years ago, had undergone significant operational changes under private management, crediting Rai Group with introducing professionalism and efficiency.
Speaking at Nzoia Sugar Company grounds in Kanduyi Constituency, Bungoma County, on Monday, the President issued bonus cheques worth Sh195 million to farmers supplying sugarcane to the factory.
The payment forms part of Sh1.2 billion being distributed to farmers across the Western sugar belt.
“Four years ago, when we stood on these very grounds and pledged to revive this factory, it was one of the most inefficient facilities in this part of the world,” Ruto said.
He noted that farmers were now receiving payments for cane deliveries within a week, while factory employees were earning their salaries on time.
“Today, farmers are paid for cane deliveries within a week while workers receive their salaries on time at the end of every month. This is a historic day for Nzoia Sugar Company,” he said.
The President added that the miller was now paying taxes to the Government and contributing to economic growth.
Nzoia Sugar Company Managing Director Tejveer Rai disclosed that the company had paid Sh1.6 billion to sugarcane farmers this year, alongside Sh150 million to cane harvesters.
He said the miller had also remitted Sh688 million in taxes to the National Government and Bungoma County, in addition to Sh639 million in lease and concession fees.
Rai further revealed that the company was investing Sh5.7 billion in factory modernisation, with some of the new equipment already in transit.
The President maintained that Nzoia Sugar Company remained the property of the people of Bungoma, dismissing claims by opposition leaders that the Government had surrendered ownership of the facility through the leasing arrangement.
“We have an agreement with the operators of this facility. The factory and the nucleus estate will continue to be the property of the people of Bungoma,” he said.
Ruto cautioned politicians against using the company’s previous challenges for political expediency, arguing that the ongoing transformation demonstrated the Government’s commitment to reviving the sugar industry.
“Wake up and smell the coffee. Nzoia has changed for the better, forever,” he said.
He maintained that his administration had fulfilled its commitment to restore the factory, recalling the promise he made to farmers at the same venue.
The President also pledged to double bonus payments to Nzoia farmers next year as the company’s performance and profitability improve.
Ruto announced that he would issue bonus cheques to farmers supplying Mumias Sugar Company next week, with similar payments planned for farmers supplying Chemelil, Muhoroni, Miwani and Sony sugar factories.
He observed that sugarcane farming had previously become unprofitable for many farmers, who would deliver their produce only to be informed that they owed money to the millers.
The President said the sector had significant room for expansion, noting that national sugar production stood at 790,000 metric tonnes last year.
He projected production would rise to 900,000 metric tonnes this year, putting the country on course to achieve the target of 1.2 million metric tonnes required to attain sugar self-sufficiency.
Ruto said growth in the agricultural sector was translating into improved earnings and better livelihoods for farmers.
“Our competitors who are trying to lie to Kenyans that we are doing nothing, we are waiting for you with a track record of performance and delivery,” he said.
On infrastructure, the President announced that the Government would soon begin dualling the Malaba-Kimaeti section of the Eldoret-Malaba Highway at a cost of Sh3 billion.
He said the project would complement ongoing construction of the Rironi-Mau Summit Highway, with the two road projects expected to meet in the middle.
“As work on the Rironi-Mau Summit Highway continues, we will begin here so that the two projects meet in the middle,” he said.
Those present included National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula, Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, Cooperatives Cabinet Secretary Wycliffe Oparanya, Bungoma Governor Ken Lusaka, Members of Parliament and other leaders.

PRESS REVIEW – Monday, November 23: Papers react to the breakdown of the COP31 climate talks. Israeli paper Haaretz reports on the struggles of crossing the Qalandiyah checkpoint. The New York Times talks about the mathematical "formula to stop the apocalypse". Finally, the Bond universe keeps making headlines.
"The Fossilised COP" reads the headline of the Catholic paper La Croix. An editorial in the same paper calls out the "stubbornness of dinosaurs" sticking to fossil fuels. Les Echos writes "COP31 turns into a fiasco". British paper Metro has another catchy headline: "Complete COP-out: It's all hot air as climate talks collapse". An analysis piece in the Guardian writes that COP31 failed, but in "the real world, the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable". The Guardian interviewed a Brazilian Indigenous leader who said that the summit failed because leaders "refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels". An opinion piece by Der Spiegel says that "Oil-producing nations are afraid and the Europeans are making excuses". It says that renewables are posing a real threat to fossil fuels and those who make money out of them. The only option left for these businesses is to delay the process – "the longer, the better". The article says that the outcome is sobering: "Climate diplomacy is not dead, but it has reached a new low".
We turn next to Jerusalem, where the Qalandiyah checkpoint crossing has become "unbearable" for Palestinians. Israeli left-wing daily Haaretz reports that residents who work in the neighborhood of Kafr Aqab are forced to wake up before dawn and wait for hours to cross the checkpoint. About 100,000 people live in the neighbourhood and their jobs are across the checkpoint. The situation has been an ordeal since the outbreak of the war in Gaza, but it has worsened in recent weeks and nobody knows why.
Next, The New York Times tells the story of Mike Winer, a mathematician trying to solve "the last meaningful math problem of his career". This is about "how to make sure artificial intelligence behaves in ways humans want, before it becomes too powerful to control". At a conference, Winer warned his colleagues that AI is progressing much faster than we thought and "it could be heading towards a catastrophe". Most of the scientists he works with have concluded that "humans are living through their final months or years as the most intelligent beings on Earth". He is now searching for "the formula to stop the apocalypse".
Finally, British paper UnHerd says that "James Bond and GTA prove that Britain still has soft power". The Wall Street Journal writes that "James Bond's bare wrists set off watch industry war". The British spy has worn an Omega watch for three decades, but Omega's owner Swatch Group is struggling, so Pattinson might be swapping it for another brand: Jaeger-LeCoultre. The Independent, meanwhile, is interested in who is going to be the next Bond girl.
You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.
