items.text:
Atletico's Simeone breaks La Liga victories record
- Published
Atletico Madrid's 3-0 victory over Getafe may have been routine, but the win was another landmark in manager Diego Simeone's lengthy tenure at the club.
Sunday's triumph at Estadio Coliseum was the Argentine's 345th La Liga win in his 567th match, surpassing the record for the most victories in the Spanish top flight.
Simeone beat the mark of legendary former Atletico and Spain manager Luis Aragones, who won 344 matches but needed 189 more games to reach that total.
"It makes me happy," Simeone said of setting the new mark, with his side now third in the table after 10 wins from 13 games.
"I don't usually find many things to be happy about, but there is an incredible amount of work behind this."
Questioned about the perception that his team are defensive, Simeone said that was a "constant criticism we face".
He added: "I don't place much value on it, but I do take note of it.
"This narrative that we're a defensive team, as if we're always playing solely to defend. You don't win 345 matches just by defending. Is that even possible?"
The 56-year-old has been in charge of Atletico since December 2011, joining the club in an era when Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid and Pep Guardiola's Barcelona were the dominant teams in Spain.
He outlasted the pair of managerial superstars, leading Atletico into a period of consistent success and staying with his side long enough to witness Mourinho's return to Real this summer, 13 years after his initial departure.
Having won the Europa League in May 2012, after his appointment on 23 December 2011, Simeone led Atletico to the European Super Cup title three months later.
He then won the Copa del Rey in his first full season and secured the club's first La Liga title since 1996 - when Simeone was an Atletico player - in the following campaign.
Atletico have established themselves as the third force in Spanish football under his leadership, qualifying for the Champions League in every full season under his charge.
However he has been unable to win European football's premier competition, losing in the final to city rivals Real twice in heart-breaking fashion - in extra-time in 2014 after Real scored a stoppage-time equaliser, and on penalties in 2016.
Simeone's last silverware arrived in 2021 when he won a second Spanish league championship, while he also guided the team to a Europa League and Super Cup double in 2018.
His contract expires at the end of this season with the Atletico fanbase now waiting to see if their manager intends to extend his remarkable victory record into another campaign.

items.title: EACC targets youth in national campaign to promote ethical leadership ahead of 2027 polls
items.summary:
NAIROBI,Kenya, Nov 23 – The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) will roll out a national integrity awareness campaign targeting voters, with a special focus on young people, ahead of the August 2027 General Election.
The campaign will seek to educate Kenyans on the constitutional and ethica
items.text:
NAIROBI,Kenya, Nov 23 – The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) will roll out a national integrity awareness campaign targeting voters, with a special focus on young people, ahead of the August 2027 General Election.
The campaign will seek to educate Kenyans on the constitutional and ethical standards expected of individuals seeking elective positions while promoting responsible citizenship, peaceful electoral participation and informed voting.
EACC Commissioner Col. (Rtd) Alfred Mshimba said the initiative was part of efforts to address the country’s persistent leadership integrity challenges by empowering voters to scrutinise candidates before entrusting them with public office.
He said enforcement alone would not deliver ethical leadership, calling for greater public participation in demanding accountability from political leaders.
“Our message is simple: Do not just prepare to vote. Prepare to vote wisely. Do not just prepare to participate. Prepare to participate responsibly,” Mshimba said.
He was speaking during a workshop for media practitioners on integrity in leadership and elections at Whitesands Beach Resort in Mombasa.
Mshimba said the campaign would particularly target young people, whose role in shaping the country’s political future had become increasingly significant.
He cited the youth-led protests of 2024 and 2025 as evidence of growing public demand for accountable leadership, noting that corruption, high taxation and the accumulation of wealth by public officials had featured prominently among the grievances.
However, he warned against attempts by politicians to exploit young people’s political awareness by recruiting them to intimidate opponents, disrupt public gatherings and perpetrate electoral violence.
“Do not allow anyone to use you as a weapon today and abandon you tomorrow. When violence breaks out, it is often the young people who are injured, arrested or lose their lives,” he cautioned.
The Commission said it would work with the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), the National Cohesion and Integration Commission and other investigative agencies to address electoral corruption, violence and other integrity violations.
In a separate address delivered on his behalf by EACC Director of Investigations Paschal Mweu, Chief Executive Officer Abdi Mohamud said the Commission would also establish public reporting desks during the awareness campaign to receive complaints on corruption and ethical violations.
The desks will provide an avenue for members of the public to report voter bribery, public officers engaging in partisan political campaigns and other violations ahead of the elections.
Mohamud said the Commission was already aware of allegations of voter bribery during recent by-elections and pledged to investigate the claims, gather evidence and prosecute those found culpable.
He also urged public officers to refrain from engaging in political campaigns in violation of the Conflict of Interest Act, warning that those found culpable would face legal action.
The CEO further clarified that EACC’s mandate in elections is to investigate integrity concerns and submit recommendations on the suitability of candidates to the IEBC, rather than directly barring individuals from contesting.
The Commission receives more than 20,000 self-declaration forms from individuals seeking nomination as candidates during election years.
Mshimba challenged the media to support the awareness drive by giving prominence to integrity issues, scrutinising the records of those seeking public office and amplifying the voices of young people advocating for peaceful and accountable leadership.

items.title: What is crawling on Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch'?
items.summary:
Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect
November 23, 2026
Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his
items.text:
Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect
November 23, 2026
Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."
In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.
Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?
The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.
It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.
Putting microbes in the spotlight
The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."
Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."
Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.
These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.
At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.
A study in progress
At the opening of the exhibition on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the upcoming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds. That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."
People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.
Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.
But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.
"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."
The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?
Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form spores that are inactive, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."
Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.
As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.
When art and science meet
As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch'."
The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.
And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.
The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."
The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.
Edited by: Sarah Hucal

items.text:
Why is Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank under attack?
One of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions has found itself at centre of political tensions amid protests and violence by supporters of ousted PM Sheikh Hasina.
Dhaka, Bangladesh – When attackers stormed a Grameen Bank branch in Kashiani last week, they did not just damage furniture and equipment. They also destroyed records accumulated over nearly three decades.
Solaiman Morol, the branch manager in Bangladesh’s Gopalganj district, said about a dozen men arrived on the afternoon of November 18 carrying machetes, petrol and tools to break the locks. Staff members were away on field visits.
The attackers looted the branch and tried to cut open its vault with a grinder. They took out about 40 sacks of vouchers and other documents and set them on fire. They also looted steel cupboards, filing cabinets, chairs, tables and other equipment. A staff member’s rice cooker was among the items taken away. “They said that after burning the records, nobody would have to repay their loans,” Morol said.
Videos of the attack later appeared online. Morol said he heard slogans including “Joy Bangla” and “Joy Bangabandhu”, associated with ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, as well as calls to burn what the attackers described as “Yunus’s den”.
The branch has not been able to resume normal operations. Staff members have received threats and customers are worried about the safety of their deposits and loan records.
“A bank depends on trust. This is impacting our customers’ confidence. People who have deposits with us are becoming frightened,” Morol said.
It wasn’t a one-off incident.
Grameen Bank under attack
The attack was part of a wider wave of violence against Grameen Bank. Its latest internal memorandum, dated November 23, records 97 attacks on branches and offices between November 10 and 23.
The attacks have put the Nobel Prize-winning institution founded by Muhammad Yunus at the centre of Bangladesh’s political tensions, months after he stepped down as chief adviser following Hasina’s removal from power in August 2024. Hasina supporters set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members in Faridpur and Narail.
In a statement on Monday, Yunus called “the systematic assault” on Grameen Bank “unbelievably shocking”, noting that bank officials and borrower-members “narrowly escaped fatal injury” in several incidents.
Grameen Bank is one of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions. It pioneered a model of microcredit that provides small loans to people who often cannot access conventional banking services.
About 90 percent of its ownership belongs to its borrower-members, while the government holds the remaining 10 percent. It has around 10.6 million members, most of them rural women, according to its managing director, Sarder Akhter Hamed. Around 5.5 million borrowers have outstanding loans worth more than Tk19,000 crore ($1.53bn). Members also hold deposits of around Tk25,000 crore ($2bn) with the bank.
“There are many people in the communities we serve whom other banks and financial institutions are unwilling to lend to. We stand beside them and provide access to credit,” Hamed said.
The attacks have disrupted the bank’s work and left staff members worried about their safety. Hamed said the institution has around 21,000 employees and that the violence had affected them psychologically. “There is a sense of insecurity,” he said.
Is the Awami League targeting Grameen Bank – and why?
The government has blamed the Awami League, the party of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, for the attacks.
“The government is making every effort to maintain law and order,” Ziauddin Ahmed, additional secretary in charge of the political wing at the Ministry of Home Affairs, told Al Jazeera.
The attacks come amid renewed political activity by Hasina’s supporters, which has led to serious unrest in parts of the country, for example Gopalganj, her ancestral district. Hasina supporters have set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members.
Political analysts say Grameen Bank has become a symbol through which some Awami League supporters can direct their anger at Yunus, under whose interim rule Hasina’s party was banned from electoral politics. During Yunus’s stint as Bangladesh’s leader, Hasina was also convicted by a tribunal for massacres carried out against protesters who challenged her rule in 2024. Hasina faces a death sentence, but has recently asserted that she intends to return to Bangladesh from India, where she has lived in exile since she was ousted.
Mubashar Hasan, a researcher at the humanitarian and development research initiative at Western Sydney University, said the timing was significant.
“Her party has spent the week pushing for her return. Grameen Bank is the easiest symbol of Dr Yunus they can reach,” he said. “For the Awami League’s hardliners, Yunus is the face of their fall, so burning his bank is a way of hitting back at him.”
The attacks, Hasan argued, may also be intended to demonstrate that the party still has a presence on the streets, despite the ban. “Some of these attacks look like a performance of strength, especially in Gopalganj, to tell supporters ‘we are still here’,” he said.
Asif Mohammad Shahan, a professor in the department of development studies at the University of Dhaka, sees the violence as part of a broader political strategy.
He said the Awami League had two possible routes after the August 2024 uprising: acknowledge its mistakes and seek political rehabilitation, or try to force its way back into politics. In his assessment, the party has chosen the latter.
“The attack on Grameen Bank is actually an effort of sending a message of ‘politics of revenge’,” Shahan said.

items.text:
Occupied West Bank ‘military zones’ become de facto Israeli settler land
Closed military zones in the occupied West Bank are being seized by settlers and made into staging posts for pogroms against Palestinians.
Ramallah, Occupied West Bank – Saleh Zahran had a room on his family’s land with a television, a fireplace, a fridge and solar panels. The kids would play in the groves, and the men stayed up late at night watching the stars.
“We’d cook, eat, drink, spend a whole day from morning to sunset,” he says.
Zahran, 39, inherited the farmland, with 120 olive trees, in Deir Abu Mishal, a village west of Ramallah, from his grandfather and father, splitting it among his brothers.
Between 70 and 80 percent of people in the village, which falls in Area B, under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, live off the land, and just a few years ago, there were no settlers nearby.
“We’d come and go whenever we wanted, pick our fruit at our own pace, sell, build, and marry off sons from the olives. Now, it’s all gone,” he told Al Jazeera.
Since settlers set up an outpost in Area B about 1km from his land in June, nobody in his family had been able to reach it. Settlers attacked their cars, and his elderly father was pepper-sprayed while trying to reach the farmland, he says.
On November 10, an Israeli High Court decision granted the village two days of army “coordinated” harvesting, something once unthinkable in Area B.
Zahran set out with his brothers to reach their lands for the first time in five months, but about 20 settlers came at them. They threw stones, smashed the family’s truck and his brother’s four-wheeler and slashed the tyres. He saw no soldiers, and police never arrived despite their calls.
The next day, the army and its liaison office were present. But farmers were held up until about 9am, shown a map of permitted areas, and told to leave by 2:30pm. Ghiyath Nasser, their lawyer, says villagers could reach less than a third of the area in question, so Zahran could harvest only about 20 of his 120 trees.
After five months, Zahran finally reached the farm room that day only to find settlers had stolen or smashed his belongings and were drawing water for their sheep from the two wells he had restored. The saplings he had planted last year had died of thirst.
On paper, it is the settlers who are barred from the Zahran family’s property and the land around Deir Abu Mishal. But in practice, it is Palestinian owners like Zahran who are kept out.
Nasser says that after his first legal petition, the army twice demolished the outpost – which was immediately rebuilt both times – then declared the site a closed military zone for Israelis only. That, Nasser argues, means soldiers cannot demand permits or “coordination” from Palestinian owners – their job is to keep settlers out.
“Sometimes they declare an area closed to settlers, but in the application they close it to Palestinians,” said Wail Qut, a lawyer with the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), who is from Madama, south of Nablus.
Kerem Navot and Peace Now’s July report found that, at the end of 2025, farm outposts effectively controlled more than 1 million dunams (247,105.4 acres), about 18 percent of the West Bank — roughly 750,000 dunams (185,329 acres) taken since late 2022.
‘A de facto closure’
In Madama, closures came first, and the outposts followed. Qut says its northern land was never declared a closed military zone, but the effect was the same.
About five years ago, the army gated the road from the village to Nablus, citing security concerns, he says. It was the only access to as much as a third of Madama’s land. The Israeli High Court dismissed the villagers’ petition after the army said farmers could reach the land on foot or by animal and apply for permits.
“It’s a de facto closure, though,” said Qut, with farmers still barred from entering.
Then, last April, an outpost of what Qut estimates are now 10 caravans appeared inside the closed area. He said the army suddenly reopened the gate for the settlers to use. Qut and his brother were stopped by a settler in the same area when they tried to pick olives there this year, forcing them to leave under armed threat.
Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, which tracks settler land takeovers, says such closures without orders are common across the occupied West Bank. “There is no vacuum in the West Bank,” he said. “Once an area is closed to Palestinian access, settlers sooner or later will come and take it over, and this is exactly what happened in Madama.”
But Qut finds the courts complicit too. When JLAC petitioned over the outpost north of Madama in September, the court gave the state until May 2027 to respond, rather than a few days, as Qut expected.
‘On the pretext of I don’t know what’
On November 13, a wedding was due to take place in al-Mughayyir, located at the northeastern edge of the Ramallah governorate. “Despite the pain and the suffering, people rejoice,” said Samir Abu Alia, 60, a village council member whose cousin’s son, Hassan Abu Alia, 30, was the groom. But soldiers violently cut the festivities short.
“The moment the patrols came down, they surrounded the hall, 20 army jeeps, and started throwing stun grenades between the men and the women,” recalled Abu Alia. Soldiers took the groom and relatives away from his bride for two hours. Abu Alia and others say the groom was beaten.
It began earlier that day on the eastern plain, when a settler grazing his flock inside a closed military zone claimed someone from al-Mughayyir had thrown firecrackers or shot at him, although he was unhurt. Soldiers accepted the settler’s claim at face value and then sealed and raided the village. The army quickly targeted the wedding, claiming there were gunshots and firecrackers, which attendees deny.

items.title: CoG Tells County Hospitals to Ignore PS Oluga’s Directive on SHA Paybill Numbers
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 23 – The Council of Governors (CoG) has directed managers of county health facilities to disregard a directive by Medical Services Principal Secretary Ouma Oluga ordering the removal of Paybill numbers from public hospitals, escalating a dispute over the management of healthcare s
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 23 – The Council of Governors (CoG) has directed managers of county health facilities to disregard a directive by Medical Services Principal Secretary Ouma Oluga ordering the removal of Paybill numbers from public hospitals, escalating a dispute over the management of healthcare services under devolution.
Speaking durng a press conference on Monday, the Council’s Chairperson Muthomi Njuki termed Oluga’s directive unconstitutional, arguing that it undermines county governments’ authority to manage health facilities and threatens lawful cost-recovery mechanisms.
Oluga had directed Social Health Authority (SHA) compliance officers to remove Paybill numbers from county health facilities nationwide, arguing that Kenyans are covered under the national health insurance framework.
However, Njuki maintains that county governments have constitutional and statutory responsibility for managing county health facilities, overseeing service delivery and determining applicable fees and charges.
“The Ministry of Health Principal Secretary has no supervisory authority over county entities, their accounting officers, County Assemblies or governors,” he stated.
He nevertheless agreed with the Health Cabinet Secretary that patients should not be required to make out-of-pocket payments for services already covered and fully reimbursed by SHA.
He, however, cautioned against assuming that registration with SHA automatically guarantees access to every healthcare service or that all Kenyans are fully covered.
“SHA operates under defined benefit packages, tariffs, eligibility requirements and coverage limits, meaning some medical services may fall outside the scheme,” he said.
He cited excluded services, exhausted benefits, co-payments, rejected claims and specialised treatments as areas that may require alternative lawful payment arrangements.
He also raised concerns over delayed or unpaid SHA claims and operational challenges affecting public health facilities.
“New electronic contracting requirements could further complicate the participation of public hospitals in the scheme, potentially limiting access to specialised services, including cancer treatment.”
According to the Council, removing Paybill numbers without addressing these gaps could disrupt hospital operations and undermine the ability of facilities to recover costs for services not covered by SHA.
The COG Chairpeson called on Oluga to avoid making “sweeping public declarations on matters affecting county health facilities and instead engage county governments through established consultation and intergovernmental cooperation frameworks.”
He maintained that the implementation of Universal Health Coverage must respect the constitutional distribution of functions between the national and county governments.
The dispute comes amid the government’s ongoing transition to the SHA framework, which is intended to expand access to healthcare and reduce the financial burden on patients.
The governors insist that efforts to eliminate double payments must be balanced against the need to ensure that county hospitals have lawful mechanisms to meet costs for services and treatments not covered by the national scheme.

items.title: Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
items.summary:
Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous da
items.text:
Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.
Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made sea drones in the operation, which struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 invasion of its neighbor, the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.
Russian officials made no immediate comment.
The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.
Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spiderweb in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked near air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's cutting-edge drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.
At the same time, Russia's strategic bombing of Ukraine has devastated the power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.
A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.
Ukraine hits Russian assets from Siberia to Libya, Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."
"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.
Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a live video address Monday to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter in the attack, the Ukrainian leader said.
Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, using the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.
The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.
Sunday's attack severely damaged the Russian corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defense units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and the U.N. Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch Sunday's attack.
Libyan officials say two sea drones hit Russian warship
Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told The Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.
At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition on board the Russian warship.
Hours after the warship attack, another sea drone strike hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel sailing off Benghazi, the Libyan coast guard said.
Russian cargo ship was sanctioned, Ukraine says
Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, described the operation as "unique." It said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multipurpose corvette Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.
The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target, the SBU said.
A Ka-27 helicopter was on board the corvette and also went under, the SBU added.
Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.
"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.

items.title: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
items.summary:
Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in th
items.text:
Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
The claim
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
The evidence
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
The bottom line
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.
Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.
"I just get in and go," Spalding says.
For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.
"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.
The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.
Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.
That was, until she saw what it could do.
"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."
There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.
It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions, an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.
Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.
Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.
"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."
Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.
"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."
Tesla agrees. The company claims that FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.
"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."
If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.
The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.
"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.
But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.
"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."
Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.
The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.
In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musk said that "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.
"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."
Musk reposted the video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.
"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.
Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.

items.title: K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
items.summary:
K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
Parents and caregivers of young children worry the world has become less kind, and they now value empathy in their children over good manners, compassion over confidence.
Those are just a few highlights from a new survey of families' vie
items.text:
K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
Parents and caregivers of young children worry the world has become less kind, and they now value empathy in their children over good manners, compassion over confidence.
Those are just a few highlights from a new survey of families' views on kindness from Sesame Workshop, the education nonprofit behind Sesame Street.
"Caregivers see the world as much more unkind to their young children than they did in 2016," says Kim Foulds, vice president of research and evaluation at Sesame Workshop, "but the reason to hope is that parents see their children as more kind, more empathetic, more resilient than they did in 2016."
The new "K is for Kind Study 2026" comes 10 years after the original "K is for Kind: A National Survey on Kindness and Kids," and it offers a remarkable glimpse at how families' feelings about kindness have shifted, in some cases dramatically, over a decade defined by the rise of social media and bitter political polarization.
Monday's release also coincides with the debut of Sesame Street's 57th season, which will focus on kindness and compassion in action.
Let's start with that bad news: Compared to survey results from 2016, caregivers today have a much darker view of the world:
- About 80% often worry the world is an unkind place for children. That's a nearly 11-percentage-point increase since 2016;
- Fifty-four percent say kindness is not a priority for most people, a 10-point increase since 2016; and
- On a scale of 1 to 5, caregivers give the average American a 2.8 for kindness.
Taken together, the data shows a worrying shift in the way families perceive the world — as a place with more rough edges that is less attuned to the needs of their young children. To draw these conclusions, Sesame Workshop conducted 2,080 interviews in October with a nationally representative sample of caregivers of children ages 3-8 years old across all 50 states.
The good news, Foulds says, is that, while caregivers "are concerned about the division and unkindness they see in the wider world, their experience of their own children is much more immediate and hopeful."
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
This manifests in a few key ways. First, in parents' own values for their children:
- Caregivers say they value their child being considerate (68%) over being smart (32%);
- They value compassion (56%) over confidence (44%), a big swing of 8 percentage points compared to when the same question was asked in the 2016 survey; and
- They value empathy (64%) over manners (36%) — an even bigger swing of 24 points compared to a decade ago.
In short, parents and caregivers say their values are shifting toward kindness. That shift, in turn, is showing up in the behaviors families say they're seeing from their kids.
- A whopping 92% of caregivers rate their child highly for kindness, a 5-percentage point increase since 2016;
- Some 74% of caregivers rate their child highly for resilience, a 12-point increase;
- And 56% gave their child a low anxiety rating, an 8-point improvement over 2016.
And that leads to what Foulds says was one of the most startling — and hopeful — results from the survey: 94% of caregivers said, when their child does something kind, they do it on their own, without encouragement or nudging.
"The child was seeing the opportunity to be kind themselves," Foulds says. "And I thought that was an incredibly beautiful, incredibly powerful finding to see how kindness is showing up in action in young children's lives."
These encouraging numbers come with one grain of salt: It's not unusual for caregivers to have a rosier view of their own children or their own local circumstances than of the wider world. In fact, this is a common phenomenon in education research, for example, where families often give America's schools low marks but high marks to their child's school and their child's teacher.
While this phenomenon likely influenced today's results, too, Sesame's twin surveys still offer a remarkable view of how caregivers' own views have shifted over the past decade.
What is kindness? The survey offers answers there, too. Caregivers talk about their children sharing in a way that requires them to give something up, connecting across languages and culture, making room for different abilities and including children who have been left out.
The survey also includes caregiver testimonials.
The parent of a 4-year-old told researchers, "He has a child in his class that is neurodivergent, which is different than him, and he is always helpful, always kind, always says 'Hi' whenever he sees this child for class and tries to be a good friend."
The parent of a 6-year-old told researchers, "My child was friends with an autistic child who is nonverbal. My child figured out a way to communicate with him, even though he could not express himself with words."
In the new survey, 85% of caregivers say it's "extremely important" to promote kindness, which is what Sesame Street's latest season will do when it debuts today on both Netflix and PBS KIDS.
"Each story really focuses on kindness, compassion, big feelings, and it's really designed to inspire children to carry the lessons beyond the screen," Foulds says. "We want the viewing to be the beginning of something, not the beginning and end."
In one scene from the new season, Muppets Elmo and Abby realize their choices have made a playmate feel left out and alone. They feel badly and decide to comfort and include him.
As one of the show's grown-ups reminds them, "One little help is all it takes."
Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

Let's talk turkey: Here's how Thanksgiving meal costs have changed this year
If you're planning to cook this Thanksgiving, you might not be so thankful for higher food prices.
Grocery costs have risen nearly 22% over the past five years, according to federal data. Wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Trump
items.text:
Let's talk turkey: Here's how Thanksgiving meal costs have changed this year
If you're planning to cook this Thanksgiving, you might not be so thankful for higher food prices.
Grocery costs have risen nearly 22% over the past five years, according to federal data. Wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Trump administration's tariffs and severe weather across the globe have pushed up the price of food.
Still, food-price experts say it's unclear whether you'll be spending more dough this Turkey Day — and, if so, by how much.
The American Farm Bureau Federation estimates that the cost of Thanksgiving will be up more than 6% compared with last year, with staples like cranberries and dinner rolls boosting the overall cost.
The Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute found that drinks like sparkling water and wine have become more expensive but that the average Thanksgiving food bill will come in a little cheaper than last year, due in part to sales and promotions.
"But you have to be very disciplined," said Wells Fargo chief agricultural economist Michael Swanson. "You get the turkey at a great price, but then you might throw a bunch of stuff in the cart you didn't look at that carefully and find out you spent more money than you intended to."
Financial worries have pushed some people to shake up their Thanksgiving celebrations. In a recent survey by the website LendingTree, 53% of respondents said inflation was affecting their holiday plans or how much they expected to spend on the meal.
"They're doing everything from changing their food choices to couponing more and even cutting back on guests," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree.
The survey also observed a drop in the percentage of people who said they might host Thanksgiving this year: 51% expect to have company over, down from 59% last year.
Shoppers say they still want to celebrate Thanksgiving, despite the price of groceries.
"It's too high," said Philadelphia resident Andre Andrews, who is retired. "Things are high, so much higher." Nevertheless, Andrews said he plans to smoke a turkey and a roast for the holiday, even though they cost him more than previously. "I can tell you this: I know it was more than it was last year," he said.
Schulz of LendingTree said those cooking on Thanksgiving can save money by sticking to a budget, shopping around for the best price and paring down the menu.
"Nobody wants to cut back on something as meaningful as a gathering of family and friends on Thanksgiving because it costs too much," he said, "but that's what a lot of people are facing right now."

items.title: Armstrong is Everton's running man and Moyes believes he can get better
items.summary:
Harrison Armstrong's distance covered stats highlight Everton midfielder's impact under David Moyes this season
In this exclusive interview with David Moyes, the Everton manager discusses the development of Harrison Armstrong since being recalled from a loan spell at Preston North End and the reason
items.text:
Harrison Armstrong's distance covered stats highlight Everton midfielder's impact under David Moyes this season
In this exclusive interview with David Moyes, the Everton manager discusses the development of Harrison Armstrong since being recalled from a loan spell at Preston North End and the reasons why he believes the 19-year-old midfielder can still improve...
Monday 23 November 2026 10:07, UK
Harrison Armstrong has started every Premier League game for Everton this season, ranking in the top three for distance covered in the competition going into the weekend. This has been some year for a player who started 2026 on loan at Preston North End.
There was talk of a big move to Nottingham Forest in the summer and interest from elsewhere remains as Everton try to persuade him to sign a new contract. Supporters will be desperate for one of their own to stay. And David Moyes feel the same way.
"He is a big player for us," the Everton manager tells Sky Sports. "For a 19-year-old young midfield player he is doing really well. I hope he can continue to do that." That recall from Preston in January already feels like a pivotal moment in Armstrong's career.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Everton news & transfers🔵
- Everton fixtures & scores | FREE Everton highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- No Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract📺
"I was watching him quite regularly. He was doing really well and we had to bring him back. They did not like it obviously because Preston were going really well. But we had got so many injuries around December time that we needed to bring him back."
In truth, it was not ideal for Armstrong in some respects. "I think if he had got another 20 games with them it would have been good for him." But there were opportunities off the bench and the fact that he did not have things all his own way will have helped him too.
There were substitute appearances against Arsenal and Manchester City when he was brought on to help tighten things up only for Everton to concede late. But even those experiences are useful. "He is a confident boy. He has got a lot of belief in himself."
Most importantly, he has responded. "Since then he has stepped up again." Speaking to Moyes at Everton's training ground, he acknowledges that it was Armstrong's work in the summer that made him sit up and take notice. "He was very good in pre-season."
Moyes explains: "There was no way we could really put him back out on loan this year. We knew that we would find more minutes for him. But his form in pre-season games was the reason which made me think that we were certainly centred around him."
Circumstances helped. "We lost Jimmy Garner with a hernia operation in the opening games of the season, which left Hayden Hackney, who had just arrived and was still carrying a bit of an injury from last season. So it gave Harrison the opportunity to start."
In Moyes' words, it was a chance "to show what he could do" and Armstrong has done just that. "He has taken it with both hands." The youngster's obvious enthusiasm instantly endeared him to an Everton crowd that demand work rate from their players.
Those distance-covered statistics stand out but Armstrong sets the tone for Everton with his off-the-ball work. "You have got to have some attributes which are really important and that one is really important for him and for us," Moyes explains.
"He works incredibly hard for the team."
The result is that even with Garner and Hackney fit, he has stayed in. "Without doubt he has earned the right to be in the team. He has earned the right by his performances every week because we have got competition. But if you are doing as well as he is…"
Of course, Moyes remains the archetypal tough-taskmaster and it is only natural that the 63-year-old Scot opts to couch his praise for the player with a reminder that Armstrong must add more to his game if he is to fulfil his potential in the long term.
"There are things we want him to improve on. He has still got a bit to learn." What exactly? "We would like him to do a bit better with his passing at times and I certainly want him to score more goals or get more opportunities. They would be the things."
But there is optimism that he can add these elements. "We must not forget that he is a 19-year-old midfield player and very much learning his trade." Moyes knows. He has overseen the development of top-class teenagers from Wayne Rooney to Declan Rice.
What is his verdict on how good Armstrong could go on to become? "I think that he can develop into a really top-notch midfield player," adds Moyes. It has been a breakout year for him in the Premier League. But this could be just the start for Harrison Armstrong.

items.summary:

Is Gerwyn Price the favourite to win his second world title at Alexandra Palace after beating Gian van Veen in the Grand Slam of Darts final?; you can watch the World Darts Championship l
items.text:
Gerwyn Price: Wayne Mardle says Welshman knows he can win World Championship again after fourth Grand Slam title
Is Gerwyn Price the favourite to win his second world title at Alexandra Palace after beating Gian van Veen in the Grand Slam of Darts final?; you can watch the World Darts Championship live on Sky Sports from December 11
Sunday 22 November 2026 23:10, UK
Wayne Mardle says Gerwyn Price knows he can win the World Championship at Alexandra Palace again after ending his major trophy drought to claim a fourth Grand Slam title.
'The Iceman' had not won a major televised event since 2022 and may have thought it might not happen again after losing three finals this year alone.
But with Luke Littler and Luke Humphries exiting early, Price took his chance with a brilliant 16-11 win over Gian van Veen in Wolverhampton.
- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
- Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
- Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺
Price claimed Grand Slam glory for the first time since 2021 - the same year he won his sole world title, when he was forced to celebrate behind closed doors due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
"Gezzy knows he can win it. Yes, winning the Grand Slam four times is amazing for him, but he knows he can win the Worlds," said Mardle.
"He's done it before and he's got a new-found fanbase.
"He's enjoying himself and it's incredible the way that everything's turned around for him. And, look, he's enjoying life.
"It's good to see Gezzy smile."
Looking ahead to Ally Pally, 'Hawaii 501' said: "Those that are at the top of the tree right now, call it top six, top five, top four, they're the ones to beat. They really are.
"Luke Humphries, Luke Littler, Gezzy Price.
"Let's be honest, we know that he got beat [in the semi-finals] and didn't play great but Michael van Gerwen shone this week.
"Don't rule out a fourth world title for him. With timing and a bit of luck, anyone can win."
'Price is talking about the next one already'
Mark Webster said it does not look like Price is done after returning to the winners' circle with his eighth major title.
Price will be eyeing further televised success at the Players Championship Finals which takes place at Butlin's Minehead Resort from November 27-29.
Van Veen, Humphries and Van Gerwen will also headline, as a 64-player field compete in the final tournament before the 2027 World Darts Championship.
"He's still got tournaments to win. He's talking about the next one already," said Webster.
"He goes to Minehead and he's talking about this trend with winning this and winning the Worlds.
"He wants another World Championship, and particularly all the heartache he's had getting to finals this year, to get over the line, really important for him. It could open up some floodgates for him now to go on and win major after major."
The 2008 Lakeside world champion believes the cream will rise to the top on the grandest stage of them all.
"At the Worlds, there'll be upsets, but I think it will come to the top players," said Webster as Price aims to follow Michael Smith, Humphries and Littler - twice over the past four years - to win the Slam and then go on to win the Worlds in just over a month.
"I think the two Lukes left this event - they just got beat by the better player. There's no real concern in the way they played, so they'll be a force, along with Price, Gian, and it's good to see Michael [Van Gerwen] in glimpses, but it's going to be a brilliant three weeks at Ally Pally."
Has winning the Grand Slam done Price a huge favour?
Victory for Price means he is provisionally up to world No 3, with Littler still No 1, Van Veen at No 2, and Humphries down to No 4 - potentially shaking up the draw heading into the Worlds.
Price, who took home the £200,000 jackpot in Wolverhampton, has also overtaken Littler with the most ranking money earned this season.
Commentator Dan Dawson explained: "Price has had to battle to this title, and I think he's had to battle to win this Grand Slam more than he has in any other since his first, because we've seen him play unbelievable stuff to win Grand Slam titles.
"But I think that's what he's had to do to become a winner again, and seeing him smile and seeing that pressure lift, just hearing him talk, I think that is an enormous sign because he's already looking ahead. What can I win next?
"We know that at Ally Pally he is up into No 3 in the world, with Humphries and Littler on the same side of the draw provisionally.
"That game there between Gian and Price, that would provisionally be the semi-final in the other half of the draw.
"So that has done him a favour if he is looking to become a world champion again."
Sky Sports remains the home of darts with the World Championship (December 11-January 3) live. Stream darts and more through NOW with no contract.

items.title: Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis
items.summary:
Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia and bipolar disorder diagnosis ahead of Anthony Joshua fight
Tyson Fury has opened up on being diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in a new feature-length Netflix documentary; Fury was diagnosed following his victory against Wladimir Klitschko in 2015;
items.text:
Tyson Fury reveals schizophrenia and bipolar disorder diagnosis ahead of Anthony Joshua fight
Tyson Fury has opened up on being diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in a new feature-length Netflix documentary; Fury was diagnosed following his victory against Wladimir Klitschko in 2015; he is preparing to fight Anthony Joshua on December 11
Monday 23 November 2026 11:54, UK
Tyson Fury has opened up about being diagnosed with schizophrenia following his ascent to becoming world heavyweight champion in 2015.
Fury is set to end his long wait to fight Anthony Joshua on December 11, and ahead of the blockbuster British bout, a new feature-length Netflix documentary, TYSON FURY, will shed light on his career and his mental health struggles.
Fury defeated Wladimir Klitschko in November 2015, and was due to fight the Ukrainian again in October 2016, but withdrew after being declared "medically unfit to fight".
- Harrison: Fury and Joshua have a genuine animosity
- Joshua unable to see new daughter until after Fury fight
- Read the latest, news, updates and video ahead of Fury vs AJ
After his victory against Klitschko, the 'Gypsy King' revealed he had struggled with drug and alcohol addiction and had gained weight.
He was admitted to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack, and revealed that while in hospital he had heard voices in his head.
"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury said during the Netflix documentary, which is due to air on November 27.
"It was like a living version of the pits of hell.
"I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.
"The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder."
During his stay in hospital, Fury explained he believed the "radio started talking to me" and voices had threatened to kill him and his family.
His wife Paris, whom he married in 2008, visited her husband in hospital and was told by doctors that the British fighter had suffered an anxiety attack.
"I was so scared, scared for him. I could see he was gone, he'd flipped the switch," Paris said.
Paris added: "[The doctors said] he's a mild schizophrenic and even then, the penny didn't drop.
"I was like: 'Don't be silly, what's she on about schizophrenic? Maniacs are schizophrenic, you're not schizophrenic'.
"I'd never heard of bipolar. When someone actually explained it to me, it was: 'Wow, that's him to a T'."
The NHS says Schizophrenia is a long-term mental health illness that is a form of psychosis.
Those suffering from the condition may, at times, be unable to distinguish their own thoughts from reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations and delusions.
The NHS describes bipolar disorder as a mental health issue where a person can experience extreme changes in their mood.
Fury, who has been open about his struggles with mental health in the past, spoke during the documentary about how he would go on to seek professional help for his condition.
He would return to professional boxing three years after his victory over Klitschko, before winning the WBC world heavyweight belt with a victory over Deontay Wilder in December 2018.
During the documentary, Fury credits his family for helping him through that period.
"If you look at my life, there's a lot of achievements, a lot of good stuff, a lot of success," he said.
"But the most successful thing I have in my life is my family, my kids and my wife."

items.summary:
'Let down on all sides': Pacific island nations express despair over COP31 failure
Several Pacific island nations expressed despair and disappointment Monday over the failure of the UN climate talks to reach a final agreement on tackling the climate crisis. Small nations in the Pacific are among the
items.text:
'Let down on all sides': Pacific island nations express despair over COP31 failure
Several Pacific island nations expressed despair and disappointment Monday over the failure of the UN climate talks to reach a final agreement on tackling the climate crisis. Small nations in the Pacific are among the world's most vulnerable to the rising sea levels brought on my man-made global warming.
The finger pointing to assign blame for the collapse of UN climate talks in Turkey began on Monday with calls for the resignation of the Australian minister leading them, while the Pacific island nations most at risk from rising sea levels expressed their despair over the failure of countries to collectively address the climate crisis.
For the first time since the 2009 meeting in Copenhagen, the COP climate conference could not reach a final agreement from its talks after the EU and others rejected a final deal that did not include any mention of fossil fuels' role in global warming because of pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil-producing nations.
This was the first meeting since the UN's environmental body confirmed global temperatures were set to exceed the 1.5°C level scientists have said will cause extreme weather impacts to intensify, and the lack of collective action has increased a sense of impotence around the multilateral COP process.
'A complete and utter failure'
Turkey hosted the latest talks, called COP31, in Antalya but shared leadership with Australia. Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen was the COP31 president of negotiations and opposition politicians in his home country blamed him for the failure.
"This energy minister's got to go because he's a complete and utter failure," Angus Taylor, a member of the Australian parliament who leads the right-wing opposition, told reporters on Monday.
"Chris Bowen was responsible for it. He should go," Taylor said.
Speaking after the COP31 talks, Bowen blamed the very strong red lines many parties had on climate change.
The climate minister maintained the summit backdrop was "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory", as soaring energy prices and fallout from the Middle East war complicated the search for unity.
Under pressure to show progress in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal, Bowen sought an overarching "cover decision" to prove countries were still united in tackling the crisis.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
But his plan unravelled as familiar fault lines emerged over fossil fuels, with the EU and Saudi Arabia locking horns over the pace of the shift away from coal, oil and gas.
"We will not endorse a cover decision ... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.
"And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."
Inside the Australian parliament, other opposition members asked centre-left Prime Minister Anthony Albanese why he would not sack Bowen after the country had spent A$150 million ($99.23 million) on COP31.
Albanese did not comment directly on whether he would ask Bowen to step down.
"We believe that climate change is real. We believe in the science," Albanese said. "Whether it's environmental security or national security, we act in Australia's national interest."
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels "the way of the dinosaurs" during a fiery appearance at the talks, expressed deep dismay.
"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," the outgoing UN chief said in a statement.
Green transition is 'irreversible'
The COP31 talks began on November 9 but the lack of a final agreement extended the summit to a record overtime on Sunday.
There was already some contention before their start as Australia fought with Turkey over hosting duties.
More than 190 countries were represented, and more than 92,000 people had registered, making it provisionally the largest UN climate conference on record. The United States did not send a delegation.
Last year's talks in Belem, Brazil, produced a deal but no commitment to phase out fossil fuels.
China voiced disappointment on Monday.
"We express our disappointment over this, while maintaining that confidence in the multilateral process should not be lost as a result," foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news briefing.
Guo added that addressing climate change is a "shared undertaking for humanity" and stressed that the global trend toward low-carbon development is "irreversible".
Read moreCOP31: Betting on electricity to break the climate deadlock
Most Pacific island nations, which are facing rising sea levels and other existential threats from climate change, expressed deep disappointment.
"We have been let down on all sides," the delegation from the Marshall Islands at COP31 said in a statement.
Tuvalu, the Pacific island nation that hosted a pre-COP event in October highlighting its exposure to rising sea levels, called out the absence of engagement and transparency in trying to reach a decision on a final statement.
"Listening to parties who diminish the credibility of signs of climate change is disappointing," said Maina Talia, Tuvalu's climate minister, expressing concern about the lack of commitment to put the world back on track for the global temperature goal.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)
