items.summary:
At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks
At least 15 people are killed in multiple attacks, days after Russian President Putin promises a ‘painful’ response to Ukrainian attacks.
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of
items.text:
At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks
At least 15 people are killed in multiple attacks, days after Russian President Putin promises a ‘painful’ response to Ukrainian attacks.
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.
Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly drone and missile barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter while the full-scale invasion grinds through its fifth year.
An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said on Monday.
“Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble,” Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said earlier on Telegram that the dead included a teenager.
It said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.
Rescuers had managed to pull out survivors from the rubble, including a 79-year-old woman and a child, Tkachenko said.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said people were believed to still be under the rubble.
“Rescuers are still at the site, working to try to pull people out from under the rubble dead or alive,” she said.
A Russian strike on a supermarket killed three other people and wounded 15, including three children, in Vyshneve, a city just south of Kyiv, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.
“People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries. An ordinary shopping trip turned into a tragedy due to a Russian attack,” Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in nearby Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.
Moscow has ramped up attacks on Ukraine and its energy network in particular as temperatures drop to around freezing.
Putin promised on Thursday that Russia would respond to Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule over Ukraine’s Russian-annexed Crimean Peninsula, with “much more painful” attacks.
Ukraine hit the bridge three times in a week, severing the part of it used by vehicles and halting train services.
Ukrainian attacks hit Russia and beyond
Meanwhile, drones attacked oil storage facilities in Russia’s Tatarstan region, damaging several, but there were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries, according to the Interfax news agency, which quoted local authorities.
“A fire broke out there,” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova reported from Moscow, adding that the attack targeted the facility in Tatarstan’s Almetyevsk area.
Shapovalova said drone attacks were also reported in the Novoshakhtinsk area in Rostov, hitting a petroleum products plant and causing a fire in a storage tank.
She added that an attack was also reported in the city of Perm in the Volga region, where a large oil refinery is located.
Our correspondents said the attacks in Tatarstan, which is about 1,000km (620 miles) away from the Ukrainian border, demonstrate Kyiv’s ability to penetrate deep inside Russia.
Kyiv confirms Libya attack
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine’s forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest ships, commissioned in 2023, near the coast of Libya using seven Ukrainian-made naval drones.
Zelenskyy said they hit a second target, the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara. The Ukrainian president said it was used by Russia to transport weapons.
“We continue operations in designated waters,” he said on Telegram.
Zelenskyy added that a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter was destroyed along with the corvette.

items.title: EACC: We cannot bar candidates from contesting elections
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) has clarified that it lacks the constitutional mandate to bar individuals from contesting elections, saying the responsibility rests with the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).
EACC Chief Executive Officer
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) has clarified that it lacks the constitutional mandate to bar individuals from contesting elections, saying the responsibility rests with the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).
EACC Chief Executive Officer Abdi Mohamud said the commission’s role under Chapter Six of the Constitution is to assess the integrity and ethical suitability of individuals seeking elective positions and submit its findings and recommendations to IEBC.
He explained that IEBC is mandated to determine candidates’ eligibility and register those who meet the requirements for elective office.
Speaking during a workshop for media practitioners on integrity in leadership and elections, Mohamud said the commission had faced criticism from members of the public who expected it to directly disqualify candidates deemed unsuitable to seek elective positions.
He attributed the misunderstanding to EACC’s role in verifying the integrity of individuals seeking appointment or election to public office.
Mohamud disclosed that EACC receives more than 20,000 self-declaration forms from aspiring candidates during election years and works with IEBC to establish criteria for integrity verification.
He said the commission had submitted reports containing recommendations on candidates it considered unsuitable to contest the 2017 and 2022 General Elections.
Mohamud also revealed that EACC had investigated 228 allegations involving the use of forged academic and professional certificates to secure employment or positions of authority.
He said the commission had forwarded 134 investigation files to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) for consideration of prosecution.
Of the cases, 60 are pending before courts, while 50 have been concluded, resulting in 45 convictions and five acquittals.
The commission has also recovered KSh41.2 million obtained through employment or benefits secured using forged academic and professional certificates.
Mohamud warned that elected leaders were among those investigated and prosecuted over certificate forgery, adding that the commission would intensify scrutiny of academic and professional documents submitted alongside self-declaration forms ahead of the August 2027 General Election.
The EACC chief executive further disclosed that the commission was aware of allegations of voter bribery during recent by-elections and would investigate individuals implicated in electoral malpractice.
He said the commission would gather evidence and pursue prosecution of those involved in bribing voters as political campaigns gather momentum ahead of the 2027 elections.
Mohamud added that evidence of electoral offences could also be presented in court during election petitions.
The commission also cautioned public officers against participating in partisan political campaigns in violation of the Conflict of Interest Act, warning that those found culpable would face legal action, including criminal prosecution.
Mohamud announced that EACC would soon launch a public sensitisation campaign to educate voters on the moral and ethical standards expected of individuals seeking elective office.
The initiative will include the establishment of reporting desks to receive complaints relating to corruption, ethical violations, voter bribery and public officers engaging in partisan political activities.
He urged media practitioners to partner with the commission in promoting integrity and accountability among voters, political aspirants, political parties and the wider public.
Mohamud said safeguarding democracy, peace and prosperity was a shared responsibility, adding that EACC was extending its anti-corruption efforts to the electoral process ahead of the 2027 General Election.

items.text:
‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
A new report by UK-based charity Oxfam shows how Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’.
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.
Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).
“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.
“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”
The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.
It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.
Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.
Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.
In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.
Air pollution
Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.
Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.
Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.
A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.
61 million tonnes of rubble across Gaza
By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.
The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.
Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.
The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.
The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.
Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.
A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.
According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.
Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.
Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.
Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.
In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.
July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.

items.text:
Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
November 23, 2026
Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.
In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree.
According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.
As a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW.
To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments.
Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente, or Early Start Pension.
How does the Early Start Pension work?
Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager between the ages of six and 18.
Beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current plans would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn.
Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections.
Parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement.
Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW.
"But it will not solve Germany's pension problems, which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension.
Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households.
"That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he said.
The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment.
It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens."
What does the government say?
The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth.
Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore.
Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age.
But Germany's plan differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision.
The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets.
Can the scheme encourage long-term investing?
Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), says there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets.
"The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them."
Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.
"If we start now with the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, we're talking about the 2080s. That's a bit too far in the future to be able to draw meaningful conclusions."
In the meantime, he says, the scheme's most immediate effect may be to strengthen ties between families and financial institutions, particularly if account holders make additional contributions.
Opposition parties, including the Greens and the Left Party, have criticized the plan, arguing it would reinforce social disparities and boost inequality since better-off parents could pay more into accounts.
Yet Geyer says the measure won't increase inequality per se. "Sure, wealthy families are more likely to top up their contributions more substantially. But they probably would have done that anyway," he underscored.
"A more interesting question is whether the measure can also encourage people with limited financial means to invest in stocks," he said.
What else should be done to stabilize the pension system?
Geyer points out that Germany cannot entirely escape the costs of demographic decline and an aging society.

Momanyi also called for increas
items.text:
KISII, Kenya Nov 23 – Minnesota House of Representatives member Huldah Momanyi has challenged Kenyan women to overcome barriers to political participation and seek elective positions, as she concluded her homecoming tour following her re-election in the United States.
Momanyi also called for increased investment in youth development and talent identification, urging stakeholders to create more opportunities for young people to excel through sports and other initiatives.
Speaking at Getembe Comprehensive School in Nyamira County, Momanyi, who is serving her second term representing Minnesota’s House District 38A, encouraged women to step forward and compete for leadership positions.
“I am an example of a woman who contested an elective seat in the United States and won. I appeal to women to come out and vie for elective positions,” she said.
She argued that leadership opportunities should not be left to men, urging women to overcome societal barriers and actively participate in decision-making.
Momanyi secured re-election on November 3, 2026, garnering 9,852 votes, representing 71.8 per cent of the total votes cast, against Republican challenger Charlie Kistler, who received 3,840 votes.
During her visit, Momanyi also advanced discussions on potential healthcare cooperation between Kenya and Minnesota.
She previously led a 14-member delegation of US healthcare professionals to Nairobi for talks with the Ministry of Health on a possible framework to recruit Kenyan nurses to work in Minnesota, which faces a projected shortage of approximately 30,000 nurses by 2030.
The proposed initiative seeks to explore opportunities for Kenyan healthcare professionals while ensuring that knowledge, technology and expertise are channelled back to Kenya to mitigate the effects of brain drain.
A pilot programme was conducted in September 2026, during which a group of Kenyan nurses travelled to Minnesota and secured placements in healthcare facilities.
Momanyi also held talks with Nyamira Governor Amos Nyaribo on ways the Gusii diaspora could contribute more meaningfully to improving livelihoods in the region.
Their discussions focused on potential partnerships in early childhood education, particularly digital learning, healthcare cooperation and linking young people to opportunities abroad.
The tournament launch at Getembe Comprehensive School also brought together Roots Party leader George Wajackoyah, who challenged political leaders to abandon personal attacks and focus on development agendas.
Wajackoyah criticised politicians who resort to insults against their rivals during public rallies, arguing that such conduct undermines meaningful political competition.
He said Kenyans deserved campaigns centred on policies, development priorities and practical solutions to challenges facing citizens.
“You cannot hear candidates in America abusing each other. It is only leaders without an agenda who attack their rivals verbally,” Wajackoyah said.
He urged politicians to compete through ideas and clearly articulated manifestos rather than personal attacks, particularly as the country approaches the 2027 General Election.
Wajackoyah further called on voters to scrutinise candidates’ development plans and hold political leaders accountable for their promises.
He also praised former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i for his performance in government, dismissing suggestions that the two were political enemies despite belonging to different political formations.

Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that super
items.text:
Artificial superintelligence ‘arriving’, warns top Meta executive
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang says humankind’s actions over next year will have ‘great consequence’ for the world.
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.
The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.
“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”
Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.
AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.
While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.
In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”
In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.
“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.
“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

items.text:
NATO Parliamentary Assembly convenes amid Russian airspace violations
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 23, 2026
What you need to know
- 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly continues in Berlin
- Germany's Wadephul: 'We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory'
- NATO members to discuss Russian airspace violations in Brussels
Follow below for developments from the NATO Parliamentary Assembly on Monday, November 23:
WATCH: Was Moscow testing Europe with airspace violations?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the latest violation of NATO airspace on Friday an "intentional provocation."
The incident occurred as Russia was carrying out a wide-ranging attack on Ukraine.
But it also coincided with European military drills in Poland, intensifying concerns about Moscow's intentions.
Wadephul: 'We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory'
Following the most recent violations of Polish airspace by Russian weapons, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has emphasized NATO's determination to defend itself.
"We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory," he said on Monday as the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly continued in Berlin.
Addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin, he added: "Don't be deceived: we may be a defensive alliance but we are prepared to defend our countries and our alliance."
According to Polish state prosecutors, the three objects which crashed in southeastern Poland on Friday were Russian CH-101 cruise missiles.
Wadephul said he was in close contact with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and assured Warsaw of his full solidarity.
Later, at approximately midday local time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte is expected to address the assembly before heading to an official reception with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the afternoon.
NATO to discuss Russian violations of Polish airspace
Parallel to the continuing NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, representatives of the alliance's member states are also set to convene in Brussels on Monday to discuss the recent violations of Polish airspace by Russia.
Russian drones and missiles have frequently penetrated the sovereign airspace of Poland, a European Union and NATO member, in the course of air strikes against neighboring Ukraine over the past four years.
According to the Polish government, three Russian missiles entered Polish airspace on Friday, crashing in the south-east of the country.
Airspace violations have also been reported in other NATO and EU countries including Romania, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.
On Saturday, Finland reported a suspected airspace violation by a manned Russian military helicopter near the southeastern town of Loviisa.
Moldova, which is not in the EU or NATO, has also reported airspace violations, most recently this weekend.
Welcome to DW's coverage
Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly which continues in Berlin on Monday.
Speakers in the German capital are set to include NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, joining by video link.
Later, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to officially receive Rutte at the Chancellery in Berlin.
Meanwhile, in Brussels, representatives of the 32 NATO member states are due to discuss the recent violations of Polish airspace by Russia.

items.text:
Liverpool's attack shows its devastating potential as Florian Wirtz steps up in thumping win over 10-man Man Utd
Liverpool showed their attacking power with a 4-0 victory over rivals Man Utd; the visitors at Anfield had Leny Yoro sent off early on and Florian Wirtz pulled them apart; the German is finally showing his quality in the Premier League as Andoni Iraola's attack begins to click
Monday 23 November 2026 09:44, UK
The conditions were favourable. Leny Yoro's red card after just eight minutes. A Man Utd team devoid of confidence and defensive resilience. But on Sunday, Liverpool's attack showed its devastating potential.
"We've questioned the attacking players but they looked absolutely electric," purred Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher after his former side had put four past their biggest rivals.
Carragher has been clear in his criticism of Liverpool's expensively-assembled frontline previously. In August, he suggested Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz - brought in for £240m - were part of a summer 2025 splurge which could go down as the "arguably the worst transfer window we've probably seen in Premier League history".
Under new boss Andoni Iraola, those Liverpool players are starting to shift the narrative now.
"The attacking players from Liverpool certainly turned up today," agreed Sky Sports' Roy Keane, amid his dressing down of United's defending.
Key to Liverpool's attacking play was the much-maligned Wirtz.
- Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd - Match report and reaction
- Liverpool scores and fixtures | FREE PL highlights▶️
- Want to watch Liverpool games? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
According to Opta, he created five big chances in the game. That's the most by a player in their records for that metric, dating back to 2010.
For context, Wirtz had created just one big chance in his previous 10 Premier League games this term - that came in his last outing at Crystal Palace, where he also scored his first goal of the season. His next came at Anfield, brilliantly flicking in a quickfire second for his side after Dominik Szoboszlai's free-kick to give 10-man United little hope of a result.
It's been a long wait but it seems to finally be coming together in England for the undoubtedly talented 23-year-old. "This is why they spent the money on him," said Carragher.
Wirtz's own assessment of his form gave a nod to his team-mates. "I feel very good, but I think it's also because the team has just developed and gets better," he said. "Being part of this, you also get better. I'm enjoying this."
The development, though, runs beyond just a set group of starting attackers. It's the options and variety at Iraola's disposal which can make Liverpool fans optimistic.
Alexander Isak leads the line but, without Cody Gakpo in the side on Sunday, there was the chance for 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha to step up and he seized it, assisting Wirtz and then converting Bradley Barcola's cross to become the youngest scorer against United in Premier League history.
Ngumoha's expected assists total for the game of 1.05 was the second highest by a player in a Premier League game this season. Top spot was taken by Wirtz, with 1.08.
Victor Munoz then stepped off the bench to add a fourth from a Wirtz pass - the third time the German has teed up Munoz in a Premier League game this season.
And there is still Hugo Ekitike to come back from his injury.
Liverpool are still developing and it wasn't always perfect at Anfield. They missed six big chances to further punish United, while Isak went goalless from an xG of 1.32. Barcola, too, was at times erratic, completing just one of his seven dribbles.
The quality of their opposition shouldn't be lost, either. Liverpool are the third team to put four past United in the past month.
Iraola, though, called on his side to deliver a statement Premier League win at Anfield for the first time this season before the match and his players delivered.
The challenge is to realise that attacking potential consistently in the tests to come. But with Wirtz finally starting to shine, Liverpool's future looks bright.

items.text:
Widowed amid war and displacement: Sudanese mothers struggle to survive
Widowed by war and displacement, women in Sudan face growing challenges supporting their children amid rising living costs and shrinking humanitarian assistance.
Warning: This story contains descriptions of sexual assault that some readers may find disturbing.
Port Sudan, Sudan – In Sudan’s displacement camps, the stories of residents often follow similar paths, but each loss and hardship is a deeply personal experience.
Arafa Abdelaziz endured a dangerous 15-day journey from Omdurman to a displacement camp in Port Sudan in late 2023, after losing her husband and one of her two sons, who died early in the war.
Her husband died just days after fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, leaving her to care for her remaining two children as their home city of Omdurman in Khartoum State came under bombardment.
Five months later, her eight-year-old son was killed by a stray bullet during clashes near Omdurman’s market.
“My son was playing outside the house with his friends when I suddenly heard a loud noise. When I went outside, I found that his head had been shattered by gunfire,” said the 33-year-old.
With the fighting between the SAF and RSF continuing in Omdurman, one of the centres of the power struggle between the two former allies at the start of the war, Arafa eventually decided to flee the city with her six-year-old son, who has a brain condition affecting his development.
She describes the journey to Port Sudan as a prolonged and horrifying ordeal. Near Jebel Aulia, south of Khartoum, RSF fighters intercepted the vehicle they were in and the passengers were robbed and assaulted.
“They asked every woman carrying a child how she wanted her son to be killed. I told them to kill me before they touched my son,” Arafa recalled.
When she confronted the fighters as they attempted to assault her child, one of them hit her with the butt of his rifle, leaving her unconscious for more than an hour.
“When I regained consciousness, I saw RSF fighters raping the young women who were travelling with us on the bus. Some were raped in front of their fathers. I felt it was the end,” she said.
In October 2026, UN Women reported that 12.7 million people, mostly women and girls, needed support for gender-based violence in Sudan – four times the pre-war figure.
The agency warned that sexual violence is being used as a weapon of war, with women and girls at risk while fleeing areas of fighting, in displacement camps and while searching for food, water and shelter.
Arafa said her greatest fear throughout the ordeal was for her younger son’s safety. When the fighters asked what valuables she had, she told them she owned nothing. They took two gold rings from her fingers and after severely beating her, let her continue her journey.
“I arrived in Port Sudan with nothing, having lost my husband. My son’s condition had worsened because of what we went through on the journey and because he could not receive his medication regularly,” she said.
It was Arafa’s first time in Port Sudan, so, having no family or friends there to support her, she headed to a school sheltering displaced families. She was later transferred to another displacement camp, where she now lives with her son. But reaching relative safety was not the end of her struggles. Her son’s condition fluctuates, and she remains worried about his health and future.
“Sometimes he imagines strange things because of his illness,” she said. “Yesterday, he told me he could see a lot of blood on the ground. It makes me think every day about his future with this condition.”
Arafa cannot afford his medication, so she has resorted to giving him medicine only when his condition deteriorates. She depends largely on aid distributed in the camp, as her needs and those of her son continue to grow.
“I’m afraid to leave him alone at home, out of my sight, in case he has a seizure or hurts himself,” she said.
The war in Sudan has killed as many as 150,000 people and forced millions from their homes, often to camps in impoverished neighbouring countries.
Income levels have dropped to 1992 levels and extreme poverty rates are worse than in the 1980s, according to the United Nations. Due to conscription, fatalities and emigration to other regions and countries for work, women have become the sole guardians in many displaced Sudanese households.
The UN’s 2025 Gender Snapshot found that 75 percent of female-headed households in Sudan were food insecure – three times the rate among male-headed households.
The Mashad Observatory has documented 72,202 cases of widowhood since the outbreak of war in Sudan in April 2023. That constitutes a complex humanitarian crisis which can lead to the collapse of household incomes, stability and protection systems. In the long term, it means transmitting deprivation, economic vulnerability and psychological trauma from one generation to the next.
These cumulative impacts can weaken social cohesion, exacerbate inequalities and undermine the capacity of local communities to recover from the consequences of war. This growing burden means fewer opportunities for women to work and increased dependence on humanitarian assistance, with long-term economic implications for Sudan, the group said.
“Their suffering is further compounded when women lose the primary source of household income or are forced to abandon their homes and communities without adequate financial resources or social support networks. Such circumstances may expose them to heightened risks of economic exploitation, gender-based violence, forced or early marriage involving their daughters and the interruption of their children’s education,” a spokesperson for the organisation told Al Jazeera.

items.text:
Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).
DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.
The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
- Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader 
  - Published31 October
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.
On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

items.title: EACC flags past vetting failures, calls for tougher candidate scrutiny ahead of 2027 polls
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) has called for tougher scrutiny of candidates seeking elective positions ahead of the 2027 General Election, warning that past failures to enforce constitutional integrity requirements allowed individuals with questionable rec
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) has called for tougher scrutiny of candidates seeking elective positions ahead of the 2027 General Election, warning that past failures to enforce constitutional integrity requirements allowed individuals with questionable records to secure clearance and access public office.
The Commission said 87 individuals whose integrity records were submitted to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) ahead of the 2017 General Election were all cleared to contest, despite unresolved questions about their suitability for public office.
In 2022, the EACC submitted the integrity records of 241 individuals for consideration, but only five were disqualified.
EACC Commissioner Col. (Rtd) Alfred Mshimba said the experiences raised serious questions about the country’s commitment to enforcing Chapter Six of the Constitution, which sets out the standards of integrity and ethical conduct expected of public officers.
“These experiences raise an important question: Are we doing enough, as institutions and as a country, to ensure that integrity is given the attention it deserves when electing our leaders?” Mshimba posed.
He said some of the individuals flagged in 2017 were subsequently arrested, charged and convicted of corruption-related offences, while others were removed from office through impeachment proceedings over violations relating to Chapter Six.
Mshimba warned that the failure to adequately scrutinise candidates had come at a cost to the country through the misappropriation of public resources, mismanagement of public offices and lost development opportunities.
He called on political parties to take greater responsibility during nominations by ensuring that candidates presented to voters meet the moral, ethical and leadership standards prescribed by the Constitution.
The EACC commissioner also urged the IEBC to work closely with investigative agencies and consider credible information on the suitability of candidates in exercising its constitutional mandate to register those seeking elective positions.
“Let us work together. Let us share information, coordinate our efforts and ensure that the law is applied fairly and consistently,” he said.
Mshimba was speaking during a two-day workshop for media practitioners on integrity in leadership and elections at Whitesands Beach Resort in Mombasa.
His remarks were delivered against the backdrop of growing concerns over electoral malpractice and the use of young people to advance political interests through violence and intimidation.
He said the Commission was concerned about attempts by politicians to mobilise young people to disrupt public gatherings, intimidate opponents and undermine the electoral process.
Mshimba linked the concerns to the youth-led protests of 2024 and 2025, which he said were driven largely by grievances over high taxes, corruption and the accumulation of wealth by leaders through the theft of public resources.
He cautioned politicians against recruiting or sponsoring young people to perpetrate violence, warning that those involved would be held accountable.
“There is nothing political about sponsoring violence, organizing gangs or using young people to intimidate opponents. These are criminal acts, and those responsible must be held accountable,” he said.
The Commission said it would work with the IEBC, the National Cohesion and Integration Commission and other investigative agencies to address electoral corruption, violence and other offences within their respective mandates.
In a separate address delivered on his behalf by EACC Director of Investigations Paschal Mweu, Chief Executive Officer Abdi A. Mohamud said the Commission would intensify integrity verification of individuals seeking elective positions.
Mohamud clarified that the EACC does not have the constitutional mandate to bar candidates from contesting elections, noting that the responsibility rests with the IEBC.
He said the Commission instead investigates integrity concerns and submits recommendations to the electoral body based on constitutional requirements and agreed verification criteria.
The CEO disclosed that the Commission receives more than 20,000 self-declaration forms from individuals seeking nomination as candidates during election years.
He said the EACC had also made progress in investigating the use of forged academic and professional certificates to secure public positions.
To date, the Commission has investigated 228 allegations involving forged academic and professional certificates and recommended prosecution in 134 files forwarded to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.
Of the cases, 60 are pending before courts, while 50 have been concluded, resulting in 45 convictions and five acquittals.
The Commission has also recovered Sh41.2 million acquired through the use of forged academic and professional qualifications.
Mohamud said the EACC would continue examining documents submitted alongside self-declaration forms to ensure falsified certificates were not used to obtain clearance to contest elections.
He further warned public officers against participating in political campaigns in violation of the Conflict of Interest Act, saying those found culpable would face legal action, including prosecution.
Ahead of the 2027 polls, the Commission announced plans to roll out a National Integrity Awareness Campaign targeting different segments of society, with a particular focus on young people.
The campaign will educate voters on the constitutional and ethical requirements for leadership, responsible citizenship and peaceful participation in elections.
The EACC also plans to establish public reporting desks to receive complaints relating to corruption, voter bribery and public officers engaging in partisan political activities.

items.text:
Holloway sacked by Swindon after two seasons
- Published
Manager Ian Holloway has been sacked by Swindon Town after just over two years in charge.
The Robins' 2-0 loss at Newport County on Saturday left them 17th in League Two and was their fourth successive loss in all competitions - conceding 10 goals in the process.
They have won just two of their last 15 matches going back to the start of September and, at the beginning of October, Holloway described himself as a "dead man walking" if the team's form did not turn around.
- Swindon's Holloway labels himself dead man walking 
  - Published2 October
Holloway was appointed in October 2024 initially on a deal until the end of that season, with the club at the time a place off the relegation zone.
He surpassed 1,000 games managing in English football two months later and went on to sign a new two-year deal in March 2025, having steered Swindon clear of the drop and into play-off contention form.
Promotion was the aim last season with Holloway issuing a rallying call at the start of the campaign for Swindon to be the "team I believe we can" be.
Things started well, with the Robins in the top five of the table from August 2025 and in the automatic promotion spots in February, but a run of three wins in their final 13 games saw them fall to seventh and they lost 2-1 to Chesterfield in a must-win final match of the campaign to miss the play-offs.
The slump in form has continued as the 2026-27 season started, and while they did win three of their first five league games, they are winless in their past five (four losses, one draw), scoring just one goal in that time.
More to follow.

items.text:
Europe’s hot autumn of protests is a symptom of economic breakdown
European governments beholden to corporate interests no longer have the wellbeing of their nations as a top priority.
Europe is in the grips of a “hot autumn”. For several weeks now, French students have led mass protests against underinvestment in education, teacher shortages and dilapidated classrooms.
In Spain, mass protests broke out after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years, after her rent was hiked by 230 percent by an investment fund that bought the property. She died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Now the protests are spreading: to Italy, where upwards of one million people took to the streets of 50 cities last week; to Portugal, where tent encampments have sprung up to oppose rapid hikes in housing costs; to Germany, where riot police with water cannon confronted protesters opposing the creeping extension of conscription; and most recently, to the United Kingdom, where thousands of students joined a day of action on November 20 under the slogan “Fight for our future, not their wars!”
The common thread which has sparked these Gen Z protests is the rapidly rising cost of living. In the wake of the global pandemic, the war in Ukraine, US tariffs, and now the US-Israel war on Iran, global supply chains are breaking down, sending costs spiralling.
But this is only a symptom of a wider problem. Deregulation and neoliberal policies have allowed corporations to take over not only the economy but also politics. This has led to massive wealth concentration at the top and increasing precarity for the vast majority of the European population. The impact of climate change and the rollout of artificial intelligence (AI), threatening mass unemployment, are making the situation a lot worse.
If we want to change course, we need to fundamentally rethink how our economy works. And yet we are ruled by a political class which has lost its will to govern.
Of course, our rulers still clamour for the perks of office. But they are operating within a logic which prevents them from taking the action necessary to deal with the challenges humanity faces. In this crisis, the centre cannot hold, and support for both radical right and left-wing parties is growing rapidly.
The problem is this: 40 years ago, politicians came to accept that the free market held the answer to all our problems. Governments gave up trying to manage the economy. By handing the levers of control to the private sector, they were told they would unleash the forces of competition and economic growth, free from the sclerotic hand of the state.
As the decades wore on, it became increasingly clear that the market looked less like multiple small businesses competing for customers and more like gigantic corporations forcing citizens, governments and the planet itself to bend to their will.
Power has been handed to monopolies, which have stretched supply chains to a breaking point, privatised profits while socialising costs, fuelled inequality and trashed the environment.
Key economic decisions once made by elected governments with at least a pretence of public interest in mind are today made in corporate boardrooms, with only the self-interest of their rich investors to trouble them.
When economic decisions are designed primarily to enrich the few, is it any wonder our public infrastructure is crumbling? The things we need to make life acceptable – housing, education, healthcare – have become no more than commodities from which the monopolists can profit.
Politicians are dismantling our welfare state, claiming that today we can no longer afford to care for the poorest. They have it the wrong way around. Rather, we cannot afford the rich.
In today’s crisis, some in Europe have come to accept the need for industrial strategy, for economic planning and government intervention; all tools which were abandoned at the onset of the “free market” era.
But these tools cannot be used properly without taking power back from the monopolies – fundamentally shifting the relationship between those who now own society and those of us who live in it. It requires a New Deal at least on the scale of President Franklin D Roosevelt’s policies in the 1930s in the United States.
And in some ways, our task is even bigger today. After World War II, European politicians built a new social contract: we would all share in the massive economic growth which would be unlocked as countries recovered from war and exploited the Earth as never before. With high growth, the poor could get richer even while the rich themselves did well.
In a world facing massive resource constraints, we can no longer operate in this way. Indeed, the richest countries have already used up their fair share of global resources.
One way out is to reassert Western dominance. The one economic area in which European governments will invest is the war machine. Even Germany’s steadfast commitment to balanced budgets – a commitment which it has disastrously imposed on the European Union with almost religious zeal – can seemingly be broken when the military demands it.
But military spending will not resuscitate European industry. Nor will it keep us safe. It will further empower the monopolies who soak up ever more of our taxes while bringing catastrophic conflict ever closer. This is not protecting us from invasion but protecting Europe’s ability to do what it wants, when it wants, where it wants. We cannot, any longer, build prosperity and security on injustice. The youth protests get that; just look at the explicitly antimilitary slogans on the streets of German cities.
A real solution requires a much bigger shift in thinking. We need to accept that Europe is entering a post-growth world, where society’s resources need to be fundamentally reallocated.
This change will not be easy. It needs politicians with the will and the ability to remove power from the corporations, to break up monopoly c

items.title: ‘Haaland must be worried’: Thierno Barry’s rise has David Moyes purring
items.summary: A most unexpected name sits behind the phenomenon Erling Haaland and the £125m proven marksman Alexander Isak in the Premier League goalscoring chart this season. The rise of Thierno Barry may have surprised even the man himself but stands as a fitting reward for single-minded perseverance and the r
items.text:
A most unexpected name sits behind the phenomenon Erling Haaland and the £125m proven marksman Alexander Isak in the Premier League goalscoring chart this season. The rise of Thierno Barry may have surprised even the man himself but stands as a fitting reward for single-minded perseverance and the refusal to quit.
“Fabulous” was David Moyes’s take on Barry’s last performance for Everton, when a double against Coventry took the striker to 10 goals for the season in all competitions and his team temporarily up to fifth. It was high praise indeed from a manager who does not dispense tributes freely, and can appear to be on the French forward’s case constantly, but was no more than Barry deserved for a display that also featured an assist for Everton’s third goal of the night. His six Premier League goals leave him joint third alongside Evanilson of Bournemouth and Aston Villa’s Nicolas Jackson.
“Haaland must be worried about him catching him now,” Moyes said. That line was delivered in jest but also represented a welcome departure from the position Barry found himself in this summer, and from where Everton stood at the close of transfer deadline day.
“I’m stopping, I’m stopping,” says Barry in a searingly honest video released on his YouTube channel in September. Entitled Never Give Up, the episode shows the striker doing exactly that after one miss too many during a private training session with his personal coach. He then breaks down in tears, head in hands in despair, after a dressing down from his lawyer. “Don’t give up, bro,” snaps the lawyer. “Where you come from, you can’t give up.”
Many players in that position would have buried the footage, afraid of broadcasting weakness or of the vicious comments that would invariably follow on social media. Barry told the BBC he spent three weeks worrying whether to post before deciding: “No, I just need to show myself. They need to learn about me because last season I showed a version of me that is not me. And they need to learn about me, how I train hard to be the best on the pitch.”
Barry’s openness was refreshingly well received, even online. In the episode he admits hitting “rock bottom several times last season” when, after a £27m move from Villarreal, he went 16 games without a goal for Everton and failed to register a shot on target until December. He finished his debut campaign in English football with eight goals from 41 appearances, a tally surpassed in 13 matches this season, and was often watching Beto from the bench.
Never Give Up is revealing not only for Barry’s emotional side. It features the striker having private training sessions in England, France and Morocco in the summer. The personal coach, lawyer and personal physio who make an appearance are part of an entourage that also includes a nutritionist and a chef. Barry will not be found wanting in his efforts to establish himself in the Premier League, a process well under way before Everton’s visit to Brentford on Monday night.
“His general all-round play has improved,” says Moyes. “There’s lots of his all-round play that still needs to get better but I’d say his game knowledge, his understanding, has improved. I would never do down any leagues but I think coming to the Premier League from abroad is really difficult in the first year. I think he found it difficult. The expectation on players coming in and being good immediately is built up and he’s needed time to settle.
“He still needs lots of things to make him a rounded centre-forward but there are bits of it that are getting better; he’s beginning to look more clinical. Even in training I’m seeing much better actions than I did last year. Leighton Baines does quite a lot with him, and shows him stuff to make him better, but his integration is much better now too.”
Barry can be a bewildering player capable of inexplicable misses and touches one minute, clinical finishes and creative distribution the next. Everton’s only recognised forward should be closer to Haaland’s tally of 14 club goals for the season. But it is only five years since he started playing as a striker for Sochaux, who he joined after failing in trials as a defender for Clermont and as a central midfielder with Hamilton Academical. Lyon-born, Barry did not come through the academy system in France that could have polished the rough edges. He has had to do it all for himself and, fortunately for Everton given their calamitous end to the transfer window, he has stepped up at the right time.
Moyes, far from just being on Barry’s case, believes the 24-year-old’s story can inspire others. “It should definitely be factored in,” he says of how people should judge a player without an academy background. “Also, not understanding how it works at football clubs and how you go about it. Not in terms of how you behave – he is not a problem in that department – but just how you go about your job and what is expected of you. He is still getting used to it.
“He was in France, then went to Basel [via Beveren in Belgium], then Basel to Villarreal and then Villarreal to here. He also had quite a lot of rejections before he even got out of France, by all accounts. But there is also inspiration behind that. You can show young people that if you put the work in, keep challenging yourself and keep pushing yourself, somebody might just like what they see and pick you up.
“Basel saw something in him and obviously other clubs have decided to go for it as well. We took him as a young, inexperienced centre-forward for £27m, and a year and a half ago it was probably a worse time to be looking for strikers in the market. What ones who were bought at that time have done absolutely brilliantly? Not many. We took a gamble early. Has the gamble paid off? It’s beginning to look better than maybe it did last year but that is because of Thierno’s hard work.”

items.text:
What to make of Manchester United’s utterly torrid start under Mauricio Pochettino? To go glass half full as the new head coach had only three days to prepare the side for the trip to Anfield, the hope will be that time will cast the 4-0 humbling from Liverpool as the falsest of false starts. The glass-half-empty scenario, though, is that here was an XI packed with internationals that had zero clue how to sort out a dire beginning themselves. Leny Yoro’s very early red card may have been questionable but for the wall to evaporate and allow Dominik Szoboszlai’s subsequent free-kick to arrow home was damning evidence of how immature Pochettino’s new charges are. From here it became a debacle and the players, if they have anything about them, need to apologise to the head coach, hold a meeting between themselves and demand they start taking responsibility. If not, United are heading only one way: down. Jamie Jackson
Liverpool in late 2026 feature three £100m-plus signings. Each of them enjoyed among their best moments yet at Anfield. Florian Wirtz appeared refreshed by working over the international break with Jürgen Klopp, clearly still a scouse whisperer. Wirtz scored an improvised goal and set up another among 10 chances he created. Alexander Isak exposing Matthijs de Ligt and Leny Yoro for the latter’s dismissal was the moment to break the dam. If Bradley Barcola showed that finishing might not be his forte, his assist for Rio Ngumoha’s goal evidenced there is composure to accompany lightning speed. Ngumoha showed he has the talent to fetch a similar price tag, scoring and assisting at 18 years and 85 days, the youngest Liverpool player to do so since Michael Owen versus Leeds in December 1997. If Manchester United’s performance, and Mauricio Pochettino’s bizarre selection of De Ligt, opened the door, Liverpool stormed through it. Beating United never gets old, no matter their desiccated state. John Brewin
It has been a long time between drinks for Hull when it comes to Premier League wins: three months, in fact. Perhaps that is why the celebrations were so extreme after their win over Brighton on Sunday – though the manner of it, two injury-time goals after absorbing so much pressure all afternoon, will have contributed too. It was a much-needed victory for Hull, who continue to show signs they are perhaps the best equipped of the three promoted teams to survive. The gap to the relegation zome is now five points and their win underlined why the Tigers have the two real ingredients needed to survive. Konstantinos Tzolakis produced the goalkeeping display of the Premier League season to deny Brighton time and time again, while Oli McBurnie’s late double exemplified the kind of goal-poaching Hull will need if they are to beat the drop. Keep those two areas thriving, and Hull can perhaps look upwards, rather than over their shoulders. Aaron Bower
When Yasir al-Rumayyan, over from Riyadh to watch Matthias Jaissle’s team live for the first time this season, studied his team sheet, Newcastle’s chair presumably read between the lines. There was no space for Bazoumana Touré or Aladji Bamba (who cost a combined £78.5m) on a substitutes’ bench that in Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo featured more than £100m worth of summer signings. Meanwhile, Amar Dedic and Sean Steur (a joint £50m outlay) were withdrawn at half-time and replaced by two members of Newcastle’s old guard, Tino Livramento and Jacob Ramsey. They played key roles in a renascent second half performance, with Jaissle’s revitalised team overcoming a 1-0 deficit to draw 2-2 against table-topping Arsenal. Afterwards Jaissle and al-Rumayyan chatted. “The chair analysed the game the way I did,” he said. “He knows about football.” Newcastle’s manager wants an increased say in a recruitment process currently controlled by sporting director Ross Wilson. Significantly, the goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek was the sole summer buy to feature in the second half. Over to you, Yasir. Louise Taylor
Chelsea’s injury list was no excuse for their performance in their 4-1 defeat by Leeds. They have spent more than £1bn putting this squad together and still had an £117m attacking midfielder, Morgan Rogers, in the starting XI. Leeds, by contrast, have had to be smarter with their budget and Daniel Farke has revitalised players who previously looked unlikely to flourish in the Premier League. Ethan Ampadu had to drop down a level after leaving Chelsea, while Jayden Bogle was relegated with Sheffield United five years ago. James Justin suffered a serious achilles injury not long after making his England debut in 2022 and Dominic Calvert-Lewin was close to being written off after leaving Everton in 2025. Yet Farke has found ways to improve these players. They are not fashionable names and did not cost much, but they are being coached well and are in a team with an identity. There is none of that at Chelsea. Jacob Steinberg
Enzo Maresca is still in the experimentation stage as Manchester City manager. Maybe the seven straight Premier League wins to start was a false indication of where the team are, in terms of progression in the post-Pep Guardiola era. It’s inevitable that a team will dip once the early adrenaline wears off and Maresca is finding this out. To rectify his team’s slow play and lack of energy, the all-action Elliot Anderson was pushed further forward to provide the thrust from the middle of the park, while his teammates were pedestrian. Ayyoub Bouaddi was given the responsibility of sitting, with Enzo Fernández left out. “We are trying to find different solutions, right balance, and to be more consistent,” Maresca said. It looks difficult to fit all three into the team and Maresca is yet to find the right answer after four games without a win, leaving the manager to return to the lab. Will Unwin
