items.summary:
Max Verstappen rivalry with George Russell 'a good factor' of F1 entertainment, says Mercedes chief Toto Wolff
A long-standing feud between Max Verstappen and George Russell was reignited at the Las Vegas Grand Prix; Russell criticised Verstappen following a collision between the pair in final pract
items.text:
Max Verstappen rivalry with George Russell 'a good factor' of F1 entertainment, says Mercedes chief Toto Wolff
A long-standing feud between Max Verstappen and George Russell was reignited at the Las Vegas Grand Prix; Russell criticised Verstappen following a collision between the pair in final practice; Verstappen taunted Russell after winning the race as the Mercedes driver crashed out
Sunday 22 November 2026 17:19, UK
Mercedes chief Toto Wolff says the "provocations" between his driver George Russell and Red Bull's Max Verstappen are a "good factor of the entertainment" in Formula 1.
Hostilities between the pair were renewed at the Las Vegas Grand Prix as a collision in final practice was followed by a war of words that threatens to continue at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, live on Sky Sports F1 from Friday.
After Russell had criticised Verstappen ahead of Saturday night's race in Las Vegas, the pair battled for the lead for much of the race, with Verstappen claiming victory as Russell finished ninth after a late error - made as he tried to pass his team-mate Kimi Antonelli for second - dropped the Brit down the field.
- 'He's so far below my level' - Max Verstappen taunts George Russell over error
- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Verstappen poked fun at Russell at the time over team radio and then laid into the Mercedes driver during the post-race press conference, claiming that "he's so far below my level".
Wolff, who was speaking after the race but before Verstappen had spoken in the press conference, suggested the rivalry was good for the sport.
Asked whether it was a bad idea for Russell to engage in 'mind games' with Verstappen, Wolff replied: "They have known each other so long since karting.
"I think it's probably been a bit of cat and mouse.
"These provocations in either side is another good factor of the entertainment."
Their feud has reignited almost exactly two years on from a major blow up following the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix, which saw a remarkable war of words follow an incident in which Verstappen felt Russell had pushed unreasonably hard to get him penalised by the stewards.
'Max was a deserving winner'
The collision between the pair in final practice happened after Verstappen had overtaken Russell as the pair were both preparing for push laps, which Russell felt was in breach of a gentleman's agreement the drivers have.
The stewards gave Verstappen a warning for causing the collision, which Russell accepted as an appropriate outcome, but he insisted that "somebody's got to stand up to that guy".
Asked if he knew whether the pair had exchanged words following the incident, Wolff said: "I guess in the stewards' room there was a bit of an exchange."
Verstappen drove superbly to win the race, managing his deployment expertly to immediately regain the lead on several occasions.
Wolff, who publicly courted Verstappen after it was confirmed Lewis Hamilton was leaving Mercedes to join Ferrari, was impressed by the Dutchman's display.
"I think Max is a deserving winner [of the race]. He made no mistakes, and that's why he won the race.
"He always had a response. Some very good driving."
Formula 1 heads to the Middle East for the Qatar Grand Prix with live coverage from this Friday, live on Sky Sports F1. Stream Sky Sports with NOW

items.title: 'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?
items.summary:
'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?
- Published
"It's turning into our Super Bowl moment."
Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Cur
items.text:
'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?
- Published
"It's turning into our Super Bowl moment."
Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday night.
The NWSL showpiece was played out in front of a sellout crowd of more than 19,000 at Audi Field in Washington DC, with tickets retailing at more than $300 (£229).
Ultimately, the Current triumphed 2-1 to clinch their first title, condemning Spirit to an unwanted record of three lost finals in a row.
Just a few hours earlier on this side of the Atlantic, Alexia Putellas, who last month was crowned the best player in the world for the third time at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, was scoring twice for London City against Crystal Palace in front of 4,000 people in Bromley.
It is a totally unfair comparison. After all, a championship final is the type of jamboree the USA does particularly well.
Nevertheless, women's football is booming in America at the moment, with attendance figures at record highs, more franchises joining the league and club retail sales double those of 2025.
So what is behind the explosion in popularity?
And what can the Women's Super League learn from it?
A unique history of popularity
The US is the most successful nation in women's international football.
The four-time World Cup winners (1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019) and five-time Olympic gold medallists, the nation of Mia Hamm, Alex Morgan and Megan Rapinoe, has a history of winning - and the domestic game is key.
"If anything, soccer is more seen as a women's sport [in the USA]," says broadcaster Jacqui Oatley, who currently commentates on the NWSL for ESPN.
"Women have won World Cups and Olympic Games - and the men have been nowhere near as successful."
While teams in the United States became professional in 2001 - for WSL teams it was 2018 - the top flight has taken several different guises over the years.
The current NWSL kicked off in 2013 as an eight-team competition, and has since expanded to 16 franchises, with two more joining from 2028.
There is no relegation and Kansas City's victory on Saturday means the league has had eight different winners since its iteration.
As the below graph shows, the ownership picture for these sides is far more varied than in the UK, with American sides much less dependent on their male counterparts.
Indeed, Kansas City are blazing a trail. Established in December 2020, unaffiliated to a men's side and backed by ambitious owners that include Brittany Mahomes - the wife of NFL quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Winning the championship is the crowning achievement for an ambitious franchise and such success is something independent London City hope to emulate in the UK. They are four points from the WSL summit nearly halfway through the 2026-27 season.
Kansas City were also the first club to build a bespoke stadium solely for women's football and the demand for seats at their 11,500-seater CPKC Stadium is huge. Earlier this year, Brighton announced their own purpose-built venue, planned for 2030-31.
"I think our independence is a hallmark of the league," says the NWSL's Jones Simmer.
"It is something we are very proud of. It allows us to invest in our own growth, prioritise the women's game and ensure resources are flowing to it."
It is markedly different from the UK set-up, where all WSL teams bar London City are, at least, affiliated and more often financially reliant on the men's side.
But that presents just as much of an opportunity, according to Jones Simmer.
"I know Nikki [Doucet, chief executive of the WSL] and I admire what she is building," she says.
"There's a really unique opportunity to build on the legacy of these 100-year-old men's clubs that are household names, to build women's brands that embrace the legacy but also have their own identity."
- Bespoke women's football stadiums? Why US sides are making the move 
  - Published15 March
- Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built £80m women's stadium 
  - Published28 April
An on-pitch product that delivers
Fans of both the NWSL and the WSL are spoiled when it comes to talent.
Most of the US national team play their club football at home, with the likes of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Rose Lavelle household names.
International stars such as Malawi's Temwa Chawinga at Kansas City, who came 10th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings, and former Chelsea striker Sam Kerr further enhance the league's quality.
"Where it starts is the product on the pitch," says Jones Simmer. "The quality of football has to be incredible and we have the best players in the world.
"And they are incredibly engaging with our fans. For so many supporters, their entry point to the league is they care about a particular player."
Provided the standard of competition is present, Jones Simmer says fans will return - and her confidence is backed up by the numbers.
In 2026, the average gate for an NWSL match has been more than 11,000 - only Arsenal in the WSL consistently receive a higher attendance than that, albeit the US is almost five times more populous than the UK.
On Thursday, the final few tickets for the NWSL's showpiece were retailing at $300 on ticket site Viagogo, with Jones Simmer suggesting resale tickets could be purchased at six times market value in advance of the match.
As London City and Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang put it: "The answer could not be clearer that there is an audience for the women's game."
"It's our job to hook fans by making sure they have a great experience watching a game in a venue and that's about the quality of the product," Jones Simmer adds.
"Once folks have that experience, it's a really easy yes to tune in again.
- Families v loyal fans - women's football's attendance dilemma 
  - Published30 October
Not that quality is an issue in the WSL where high-class footballers abound. Take Putellas, goal

items.text:
ISIOLO, Kenya, Nov 23 – Two people have been killed and seven houses torched in a suspected retaliatory attack in Elsa Village, Isiolo, following an earlier livestock theft incident.
The victims, both members of the Samburu community, were shot dead on Sunday night when suspected Turkana bandits raided the Elsa Ayanakore cluster at around 8pm.
The attackers reportedly set seven houses ablaze before engaging security officers in a fierce exchange of gunfire.
Police officers from Kulamawe Police Station, a General Service Unit (GSU) operations team and the Anti-Stock Theft Unit (ASTU) from Maili Saba responded to the incident following reports of the attack.
The security teams repulsed the assailants during the gunfight, although two residents were fatally shot.
The deceased were identified as 65-year-old Mzee Legeyo Leterewa and his 25-year-old son, Liki Leterewa.
Police officers processed the scene before moving the bodies to the Isiolo County Teaching and Referral Hospital mortuary, where they are being preserved pending postmortem examinations.
The attack has heightened tension in the area, prompting the deployment of additional security personnel to prevent further violence and restore calm.
The Elsa area has experienced recurring insecurity linked to livestock theft and inter-community hostilities, with at least 10 people reportedly killed in the recent wave of violence.
Security agencies have intensified operations in the affected areas as authorities move to contain the situation and prevent further loss of lives and destruction of property.

Ukraine: Deadly Russian strikes in Kyiv region
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 23, 2026
What you need to know
- Russian strikes on Kyiv region kill several Ukrainian civilians
- NATO to discuss Russian violations of Polish airspace
- Interfax reports Ukrainian drones attack oil storage facilities in Russia's Tatarstan
Below are the update on Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, November 23:
Zelenskyy says Ukraine drones sunk Russian ship off Libya
Ukraine on Monday claimed attacks on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauding the nation's defense forces for the "exemplary Ukrainian operation."
"Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It's one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
"A Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette. Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit," he said.
This comes a day after a Russian vessel, docked at the Libyan port of Benghazi, was attacked by a suspected drone.
Zelenskyy further said Ukraine was continuing "operations in designated Waters," adding that it was in response to Russia's aggressions.
Ukrainian drones attack Russian oil facilities, reports
Ukrainian drones attacked oil storage facilities in Russia's Tatarstan region, Russian news agency Interfax reported on Monday, citing local authorities.
As per the report, the strikes damaged several facilities but did not lead to any deaths or injuries.
Russia's oil industry is particularly important to its economy and generates revenue that helps fund its war in Ukraine.
Russia and Ukraine have been regularly targeting each other's energy infrastructure. Russian oil is especially key to the warring nation's economy and supports much of its military operations in Ukraine.
UN urges probe after Russian ship attacked at Libyan port
The United Nations on Monday called for an independent probe into suspected drone attacks on two ships off the coast of Libya, in what could be spillover from the war in Ukraine. One of the two vessels was Russian while the other was sailing under a Maltese flag.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X.
Libya's eastern administration did not identify who was behind Sunday's attack but said Libya was "not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war".
NATO to discuss Russian violation of Polish airspace
Representatives of NATO's 32 member states are set to discuss the recent Russian violations of Polish airspace on Monday in Brussels.
No special meeting has been called for this purpose and the discussion will take place during regular consultations, a spokesperson said.
Three Russian missiles entered the Polish airspace on Friday during airstrikes on Ukraine, the Polish government has said. They crashed in the southeast of Poland which is both a member of NATO and the European Union.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who is currently in Berlin for the 72nd annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, earlier said Europe would do everything possible to identify where the risks to Western deterrence and defense systems lie.
Russian strikes kill at least 14 in Ukraine
At least 14 people were killed as Russia pounded Ukraine's Kyiv region with airstrikes overnight, local authorities said.
In Dymer, at least 11 people died after a Russian strike hit a five-storey building, regional official Tymur Tkachenko said over messaging app Telegram. "Search and rescue operation is ongoing," he said.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service had earlier said that the dead included a teenager and a woman in her forties. Before that, it said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were "not responding or cannot be reached."
It is not yet clear how many people remain trapped in the rubble of the collapsed building.
In the city of Vyshneve, a Russian strike hit a supermarket, killing three people, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called the attack in Dymer part of "Russia's genocidal war against Ukraine....The world must stop looking away. Condemn this terror, hold Russia accountable, and act now to stop the killing of innocent Ukrainians."
Moscow has been pummeling Ukraine with nightly aerial barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter, as the invasion grinds through its fifth year.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of Russia's war in Ukraine.
Overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine have killed several residents in the Kyiv region, local authorities said on Monday morning. The strikes hit a residential building in Dymer where search and rescue operations are still ongoing, and a supermarket in Vyshneve.
This comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin, last week, vowed a "painful" response to Ukrainian strikes on Russia's Crimea bridge, right after holding a meeting with US counterpart Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping.
Meanwhile, Russian media reported Ukrainian drone strikes on the country's oil facilities.
As the war rages on, NATO member states are set to discuss Russian violations of Polish airspace in a regular scheduled meeting on Monday.
Stay tuned for all of this and more.

items.title: OPINION: Healthcare Needs Fewer Firefighters and More Strategists
items.summary:
By Aly S. Maherali
A production supervisor at a manufacturing company in Nairobi begins experiencing frequent headaches. He had been feeling unwell for some time but continued reporting for work. There were production targets to meet, staff to supervise and deadlines that could not be missed. A visi
items.text:
By Aly S. Maherali
A production supervisor at a manufacturing company in Nairobi begins experiencing frequent headaches. He had been feeling unwell for some time but continued reporting for work. There were production targets to meet, staff to supervise and deadlines that could not be missed. A visit to the doctor kept getting pushed back. When he eventually went for a medical assessment, he was diagnosed with hypertension.
His employer may eventually see the cost of his treatment reflected in the company’s medical insurance claims. The insurer will record the expenditure, and the employer will have to consider it when reviewing the scheme at renewal. What is less likely to feature in that discussion is why the employee waited so long to seek help, or whether his medical cover could have helped him identify the problem earlier.
I believe this is one of the issues we need to examine more closely in Kenya’s medical insurance market. We have become accustomed to looking at healthcare expenditure through claims reports. Employers want to understand why costs are rising, insurers are concerned about the sustainability of their portfolios, and brokers are expected to negotiate arrangements that remain affordable without stripping away useful benefits. These are necessary conversations. However, they tell us only part of the story.
The Association of Kenya Insurers reported that industry gross premium income reached approximately KSh395.3 billion in 2024, representing growth of 9.4%. Insurance penetration, however, remained at around 2.44%. The industry is making progress, but expanding insurance business should also mean improving the experience and protection available to policyholders.
One issue I encounter in discussions about medical schemes is how little some employees know about their benefits. They may have an insurance card but be uncertain about which hospitals they can visit, whether outpatient consultations are covered or whether they need approval before seeing a specialist. Others are unaware that routine health assessments may already be included in their cover.
This is not a minor communication problem. When people do not understand their benefits, they may postpone treatment, pay for services unnecessarily or arrive at a hospital only to discover that they have not followed the required procedures. Employers and insurers should not assume that issuing a policy document is the same as making someone understand their cover.
Kenya’s non-communicable disease burden makes this particularly important. The national STEPS survey conducted in 2015 found that approximately 23.8% of adults had raised blood pressure. Hypertension is often difficult to recognise because it can develop without obvious symptoms. People continue working and managing their responsibilities, sometimes unaware that they need medical attention.
The same applies to diabetes and other chronic conditions. By the time someone seeks help, the condition may have progressed and treatment may be considerably more complicated. There is room for medical schemes to do more. Screening is useful, but it should be linked to consultations, diagnostic services and proper follow-up. If an employee is found to have high blood pressure, for example, somebody should be able to explain where treatment is available, what the policy covers and how to continue receiving care.
We should also be careful not to make workplace healthcare an executive privilege. Employees in factories, warehouses, transport operations and other physically demanding jobs have health needs that deserve equal attention. A company driver may have less flexibility to attend a medical appointment than someone working in an office. The way services are organised should take these realities into account.
The financial argument is equally important. World Bank data drawn from the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database indicates that out-of-pocket payments represented approximately 24.25% of Kenya’s current health expenditure in 2023. For many households, an unexpected medical bill can upset an already tight family budget. Medical insurance should provide meaningful financial protection, not simply the reassurance of having a card in one’s wallet.
I would also like to see more attention paid to claims management. Employers should receive more than a breakdown of how much was spent. They need to understand the conditions driving expenditure, the services members are using and where delays or gaps in care may be occurring. Insurers and brokers can then have a more informed discussion about improving benefits and controlling unnecessary costs.
A more strategic approach would bring together anonymised claims trends, clear member education, timely pre-authorisation, appropriate provider networks and benefit design that responds to employees’ actual needs. This would enable employers, insurers and brokers to address recurring service problems and manage costs before the next renewal.
None of this means that treatment should take a back seat to prevention. When an employee needs hospital care, the medical scheme must respond in accordance with the policy. Claims should be handled fairly, and members should not have to struggle through avoidable administrative delays when they are unwell.
I think again about the production supervisor in Nairobi. His treatment is important, but it would have been better if his condition had been identified earlier. Perhaps he simply needed to know that his scheme provided access to a routine assessment and where to obtain one.
At the next renewal meeting, we will undoubtedly discuss premiums and claims. We should also spend time looking at whether employees understand their benefits, whether claims are being managed efficiently and whether members can access care when they need it. These are not separate issues. They are all part of getting better value from medical insurance.
The author is the Chief Executive Officer, Executive Healthcare Solu

items.text:
Zelenskyy says Ukraine behind drone attacks on Russian ships near Libya
President Zelenskyy says Ukrainian forces sank the Russian warship Merkury in an “exemplary” sea drone operation.
Ukranian President Volodomyr Zelenskyy has hailed an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war”, claiming responsibility for sinking the Russian ship Merkury off the coast of Libya.
Zelenskyy said in a statement on Monday that Ukranian forces hit a second target, the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which he said Russia used to transport weapons.
The Russian corvette Merkury is one of Moscow’s newest ships. Zelenskyy confirmed that it sank after seven Ukranian-made naval drones were launched. A KA-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed in the attack.
Volodomyr Zelenskyy said that they would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas as they are responding to Russia’s aggression. He also noted that Ukraine would continue to develop Ukranian weapons.
The Ukranian President also confirmed his forces had attacked a second ship, the MV Angara, which he claimed Russia was using to transport weapons. Libya’s eastern health ministry said all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment.
Authorities in Libya’s east said in an official statement that “the explosion occurred on board a Russian ship docked in the port… The ship was en route back to Russia and its stop was for refuelling and resupply. It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones”.
Local sources told Al Jazeera late on Sunday that the number of Libyan and Russian nationals killed in the attack was not yet known, adding that the ship was moored inside the civil sea port of Benghazi.
The United Nations has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.
On Monday, the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.
Tallha Abdulrazaq, a Middle East security and defence expert, told Al Jazeera that Ukrainian intelligence services were likely behind the attack on the Libyan port.
“There was a lot of reporting at the tail end of last year about there being a deal between the Ukrainian intelligence services and the Tripolitan government to establish a Ukrainian military and intelligence presence there,” Abdulrazaq said. “In exchange, the Tripoli government would get Ukrainian military expertise.”
The eastern administration did not identify who was behind Sunday’s attack but said Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.
The oil-rich nation of Libya has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

items.title: Dr Hesbon Owilla | Beyond slogans, Usawa ni Sawa must change lives
items.summary: I recently traversed the country and spent time listening to people. While politicians campaign and coin catchy slogans, what ultimately matters is how they allocate and distribute resources. At its core, politics is about who gets what, where, when, and how. When leadership directs resources toward
items.text:
I recently traversed the country and spent time listening to people. While politicians campaign and coin catchy slogans, what ultimately matters is how they allocate and distribute resources. At its core, politics is about who gets what, where, when, and how. When leadership directs resources towards communities that have historically felt marginalised, expands opportunities and gives them a more equitable stake in national development, it shapes how those communities view government and its record.
These conversations reinforced my interest in whether, beyond slogans and political contestation, Kenyans are experiencing fairness, inclusion and opportunity, and how those experiences inform their assessment of leadership and the person they will vote for in 2027.
In Western Kenya, many people I engaged appeared to appreciate both direct economic support and infrastructure investments. Some spoke positively of what they described as politicians responding directly to everyday economic struggles through cash transfers, support for small businesses and other assistance that helps households meet immediate needs. For others, change was visible in major infrastructure, particularly roads communities say they have demanded for generations.
These responses point to an important dimension of Usawa ni Sawa. For communities that have long felt overlooked, equity is experienced not only through development opportunities and public infrastructure, but also through redistribution that can improve livelihoods now.
Our politicians appear to have perfected the art of “gather all, scatter none”. They are appealing to voters through interventions addressing immediate needs, while also using infrastructure to reach those who value capital investment and longer-term development. Both approaches shape how communities experience fairness, inclusion and responsive leadership.
Alongside this dual approach, the Fifth Administration appears to be selling what political risk analyst Dismas Mokua describes as political presence. Across the areas I visited, people associated changes in their economic or infrastructural circumstances with President William Ruto and government officials they see and hear regularly. They cited the Nyota Fund, economic empowerment drives and initiatives associated with Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo. Whether through political leaders or bureaucrats, visibility appears to reinforce the perception that government is present and responding.
Further north, however, the conversation changed. There, resource allocation is discussed in terms of equity and what a friend from Wajir calls the real manifestation of Usawa ni Sawa. Beyond roads and connectivity, the Northern Frontier counties of Wajir, Mandera and Garissa have experienced a significant expansion in teacher-training opportunities. A region that once had one functional teachers’ college now has six.
Wajir has four: Wajir Teachers Training College in Wajir Town, Eldas TTC, Tarbaj TTC and Kutulo TTC in Wajir West. Garissa has Garissa TTC, while Mandera has Mandera TTC. Together, the institutions have 4,616 students enrolled. At a graduation ceremony this month at Wajir TTC, 572 teachers completed their training.
The story began locally. In 2015, when insecurity prompted non-local teachers to leave Wajir and schools were left without staff, the county government, under Governor Ahmed Abdullahi, established Wajir TTC rather than wait for Nairobi. The county offered a 100 per cent bursary to the pioneer class. It was a declaration that if the centre could not train teachers for the region, the county would take the initiative.
That was bold leadership, but sustaining a national teaching service requires more than local initiative. Since 2022, the Fifth Administration has given the effort national backing through the operationalisation and staffing of the institutions. The result is a pathway for local young people to train and teach in their own communities.
Anyone familiar with teacher recruitment understands the old cycle. Teachers were posted to remote counties, often from other regions, and required to remain for years. But insecurity, isolation or other pressures could prompt them to seek transfers. Children in these counties consequently faced disruptions and unequal access to education. Governor Abdullahi’s vision in 2015 was therefore more than the establishment of a college. It was an investment in a locally rooted workforce.
Today, opinion leaders in the Northern Frontier counties point to 4,616 students enrolled in teacher-training colleges, 1,800 local teachers employed by the Teachers Service Commission, and the 572 graduates from Wajir TTC. The county’s 100 per cent bursary for the pioneer class helped lay a foundation for generations of local teachers. The promise is that daughters and sons of the region will teach its children and potentially those across the wider country.
This is how many residents understand Usawa ni Sawa in education. The old model recruited a teacher elsewhere, posted them to Wajir and hoped they would stay. The emerging model builds training capacity locally, equips young people with qualifications and creates a workforce with roots in the communities it serves. A teacher whose home is in Wajir is less likely to seek transfer because of distance from family or unfamiliarity with the region.
The approach is not a substitute for security, quality facilities or adequate funding. But it is more sustainable, dignified and practical than relying indefinitely on external recruitment. Equity is not simply ensuring that every county receives a road or a project. It is addressing the barriers that have denied communities equal access to opportunity.
In the North, Usawa ni Sawa is being measured in classrooms, trained teachers and the possibility that a child’s birthplace will no longer determine the quality of education they receive. That, ultimately, is what equitable resource allocation should mean

items.title: China’s Import Expo Highlights Opportunities in a Changing Global Trade Landscape
items.summary: At a time when global commerce is being reshaped by geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain adjustments and changing trade policies, China is placing market access and international cooperation at the centre of its economic engagement. The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), held in Shangha
items.text:
At a time when global commerce is being reshaped by geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain adjustments and changing trade policies, China is placing market access and international cooperation at the centre of its economic engagement. The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), held in Shanghai from November 5 to 10, provided a platform for international businesses to explore opportunities in one of the world’s largest markets.
The scale of this year’s event was significant. Organisers said 4,142 overseas exhibitors participated, the highest number in the expo’s history, with exhibition space exceeding 440,000 square metres. More than 480 products and technologies made their global, Asian or China debuts, while more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders were represented. The figures underscore the expo’s growing role in connecting international suppliers with Chinese buyers.
The CIIE reflects China’s proposition that its economic development can generate opportunities for businesses worldwide. Official customs data show that China’s goods imports and exports reached 39.94 trillion yuan in the first nine months of 2026, an 18.8 per cent year-on-year increase. As a major consumer and manufacturing market, China continues to create demand for foreign goods, expertise, technology and innovation.
Commercial agreements reported during the expo illustrated this potential. GE Aerospace said it signed sales and service agreements worth more than 12.9 billion US dollars during the event, including an agreement for engines for China Eastern Airlines aircraft. While company-reported agreements demonstrate the commercial opportunities associated with the expo, they should be distinguished from the aggregate value of intended deals, which reflects a broader measure of business commitments.
The CIIE’s reach also extends beyond multinational corporations. Across its first eight editions, nearly 13,000 overseas micro, small and medium-sized enterprises have participated. Syrian entrepreneur Muhannad Shakally first brought traditional soap to the expo in 2018 to test the market. His monthly orders later exceeded five tonnes, equivalent to approximately 20,000 bars, according to Chinese media. His experience demonstrates how participation in a major trade platform can help smaller businesses expand their market reach and export opportunities.
For Africa, China’s commitment to market access carries particular significance. Since May 1, China has applied zero-tariff treatment to imports from all 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations. The initiative is intended to ease access for African products, although exporters must still meet market standards, maintain consistent supply and establish distribution networks to compete effectively.
African participation at this year’s expo offered a practical illustration of the opportunity. Standard Bank led a delegation of 20 businesses from seven African countries, including Kenya, Ghana, Nigeria, Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi and South Africa. Their products included coffee, cocoa, tea, wine, avocados, cashews, sesame and grains. The delegation, alongside an expanded Asia-Africa Products Zone, sought to connect exporters with potential buyers and investors.
Growing trade presents opportunities, but Africa must also strengthen its capacity to take advantage of them. China-Africa trade reached 312.11 billion US dollars in the first nine months of 2026, up 22 per cent year on year, according to customs figures reported in November. However, African exports to China continue to trail Chinese exports to the continent. In the first eight months of the year, the trade deficit stood at about 80 billion US dollars. Zero tariffs offer a significant opening, but translating market access into a broader and higher-value African export base remains a challenge.
The priority must be moving up the value chain. African businesses can use access to Chinese consumers to expand food processing, improve packaging and quality standards, and develop products with greater local value. Governments must invest in infrastructure, certification systems, logistics and export finance. China’s demand, manufacturing experience and commercial connections can support this ambition, but African producers must build the capacity to supply consistently and competitively.
Cooperation also extends beyond agricultural exports. Chinese machinery, renewable-energy equipment and digital technologies can help African businesses modernise production, improve efficiency and widen access to electricity. Trade and investment partnerships will be more sustainable when they support local manufacturing, technology adoption and skills development rather than simply exchanging raw materials for finished goods.
The CIIE therefore represents more than an annual exhibition. It is part of China’s effort to widen channels for imports and connect international businesses with its domestic market. Record participation and reported commercial agreements demonstrate interest, but the expo’s real value will be measured by repeat orders, durable partnerships and the extent to which businesses can turn opportunities into sustained commercial activity.
For African exporters in particular, the opportunity is real, but it is not automatic. Taking advantage of China’s market opening will require ambition, competitiveness, investment and sustained effort. The CIIE provides a platform for international cooperation and shared growth, but turning that promise into lasting gains will depend on what businesses and governments do beyond the exhibition halls.

items.text:
MotoGP maestro Marquez makes history with eighth premier-class world title
His eighth success in the premier class of motorcycling pulled Marc Marquez level with Italian great Giacomo Agostini.
Spaniard Marc Marquez has been crowned MotoGP world champion for a record-equalling eighth time, screaming with joy at the Portuguese Grand Prix after a remarkable comeback this season.
Ducati rider Marquez finished eighth on Sunday as Italian Marco Bezzecchi rode to victory in southern Portugal, but it was enough to seal a second consecutive world title.
On crossing the line, the 33-year-old Marquez leapt from his bike and was hoisted up by his team before he ran towards his fans screaming with his arms aloft.
“We need to be happy. I know that we are here celebrating a historic moment. I know how I suffered,” said an emotional Marquez, who underwent double surgery midway through the season.
“I know that in the middle of the season, the fans believed more than I did. My people believed more than I did. But I kept pushing; I kept doing my best.
“I said last year that it was a championship where I was at peace with myself. This one is for all the fans that believed in me from 2020 until now. So thanks to all of you, this is for all of you.”
His eighth success in the premier class of motorcycling pulled Marquez level with Italian great Giacomo Agostini, who won his titles between 1966 and 1975.
As a final flourish, the Spaniard ascended a staircase accompanied by the silhouette of a goat on the screen, a nod to his growing ‘Greatest of All Time’ status, before receiving a golden commemorative helmet from Agostini himself.
He then attached another plaque with his name engraved on it on the Tower of Champions before embracing and lifting it over his head.
Marquez’s latest triumph is even more remarkable given the Spaniard’s injury- and crash-blighted campaign in which he had to wait until the eighth race in Hungary on June 7 before claiming his first win.
Marquez suffered a flat tyre in the season-opener in Thailand in March, fell at the Spanish GP in Jerez and again at the French GP where he picked up a foot fracture which ruled him out of the following race, the Catalan GP.
Making his comeback at the Italian GP in Mugello, he trailed Bezzecchi by 102 points in early June, just weeks after undergoing foot surgery on top of a previous operation on his injured shoulder.
But the Spaniard managed to bounce back once again, defying those who had already written him off.
Once he got rolling, he roared into a regular winning run with seven Grands Prix and 10 sprint race victories in all this season.
While not as obviously dominant as winning 11 GPs in the 2025 season, when an unexpected return to form following his 2024 switch to Ducati gave him a new lease of life, the latest win is as impressive.
Marquez had been the youngest-ever premier-class champion in his debut season in 2013 for Honda and then went on to win the title in five of the next six seasons.
He also overtook his great rival Valentino Rossi, who won seven MotoGP titles, although the swashbuckling Italian has 89 individual race wins in the top category compared with Marquez’s 80.
Having crashed during Saturday’s sprint race, Marquez rode out Sunday’s GP safely, needing only to finish in the top nine to secure his 10th title across all categories combined.
Aprilia’s Bezzecchi won Sunday’s race to complete the double in Portugal, having also won the sprint, with his stablemate Jorge Martin of Spain crossing in second.
With a total of 439 points and seven victories this year, this was enough for Marquez to keep his rivals at bay.
Martin is second with 396 points but only one win, and Bezzecchi, who has 394 points and seven first-place finishes, is third ahead of the season finale in Valencia, Spain, next weekend.
“Thank you for this bike,” Marquez told his team Ducati during his victory lap.

items.text:
Germany news: Metalworkers go on strike as pay dispute heats up
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 23, 2026
What you need to know
- Germany's biggest union IG Metall is calling for metal workers to go on strike, affecting factories across much of northern Germany. It centers around a pay dispute that's been heating up for weeks
- German President Frank Walter Steinmeier heads to several African countries for a 4 day visit focusing on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers
- A fire at a Berlin hospital has left at least 15 people injured with the police suspecting arson
- A key survey is expected to give insights about how Germans are thinking about foreign policy issues at a time of intense geopolitical tensions.
Read below for more on these stories and all other things Germanyon Monday, November 23.
Germany criticises oil states over failure to adopt climate resolution
The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.
"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.
Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.
Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention plans to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.
"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.
The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.
German President Steinmeier starts Africa trip
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.
He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.
In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."
His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.
The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.
The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.
Patient suspected of starting fire in Berlin hospital
Police are investigating a suspected case of aggravated arson after a fire broke out at a hospital in Berlin.
Investigators believe a patient set fire to his bed in a room on the first floor of one of the hospital buildings in the Lichtenberg district on Sunday evening.
One nurse and the suspected arsonist suffered smoke inhalation and had to be treated in hospital. Overall, 15 people were injured with another 13 suffering from minor injuries.
While firefighters managed to put out the flames, smoke spread to other parts of the hospital which then had to be evacuated.
Widespread strikes expected across Germany
The country's largest and most powerful union, the IG Metall, has called for a strike this Monday over an ongoing pay dispute.
The union has called on some 23,000 workers to down tools in as many as 19 factories in northern Germany. Among the companies affected likely to be impacted are Siemens, Mercedes Benz, and shipyard Meyer Werft.
At a similar strike on Friday, more than 12,000 workers had taken part.
IG Metall hopes that the strikes will increase pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% wage increase.
Employers have so far offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.
Welcome to our coverage
Welcome and guten Morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn!
Another busy week is kicking off and in large parts of Germany it starts with workers are walking off the job today in what is becoming a very heated dispute over pay. Factories from Mercedes Benz to the large shipmakers will likely be affected.
Berlin woke up this morning to news of a fire in the Lichtenberg part of the city, leaving at least 15 people injured. Police have described it as a serious case of arson.
And the country's president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is off for a trip to Africa which over the next few days that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.
We'll cover all those stories and whatever else hits the headlines across Germany so stay tuned.

items.text:
India-Pakistan cricket fans want ‘dirty politics’ kept out of beloved sport
Cricket's die-hard fans say players are being forced to partake in aggression for the benefit of politicians.
India-Pakistan cricket rivalry brings World Cup atmosphere to Qatar
Doha, Qatar – Heated exchanges, scowling faces, body shoves, handshake controversies and trophy ceremony boycotts.
Cricket fans from India and Pakistan are no strangers to seeing their teams throw childlike tantrums on the field. Some even believe it’s the fire that fuels sport’s fiercest rivalry.
On Sunday, when the nations met in the Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 in Doha, the temperature on the pitch matched the typically hot Middle Eastern afternoon.
Not long after Pakistan opted to bat first, India’s fast bowler Harshit Rana and Pakistan’s top-order batters were involved in what did not seem like a friendly exchange. Verbal blows were exchanged and dismissed batters were given hostile send-offs.
The trend continued during India’s innings, which ended 48 runs short of the target, giving the Pakistanis a rare victory over their neighbours.
In the stands, though, the supporters were following a different script.
It took a few hours for the West End International Cricket Stadium to fill up – with Sunday being the first working day of the week in Qatar – but towards the second half of the match, the attendance came close to its 10,000-person capacity.
Supporters of both countries, as well as neutral cricket fans, mingled in the stands while wearing their respective teams’ shirts, waving their own countries’ flags and chanting their players’ names.
‘Worrying signs’
For many, such as Abrar Hussain and Mohammed Saeed Khan, there didn’t seem to be a need for segregation while watching a sport both nations follow with equal fervour.
“We have been friends for over six years,” Khan told Al Jazeera.
Wearing a replica blue shirt of the Indian team, Khan sat next to his Pakistani friend Hussain, dressed in Pakistan’s shirt.
“We share accommodation, meals and a love for the game that goes beyond any rivalry,” the man from India’s southern port metropolis of Mumbai explained.
Khan and Hussain, who are teammates in a weekend cricket league in Doha, expressed their disappointment at the “politicisation of the sport.”
“Politics should stay out of the game,” said Hussain, a native of Pakistan’s largest city, Karachi.
“The game of cricket is very close to our heart. We don’t want anything spoiling our game.”
Recent cricket encounters between the two nations – at all levels, from senior men’s teams to women’s sides, as well as age-group teams – have been heavily politicised following their intense four-day conflict last May.
Four months after both countries returned from the brink of all-out war, their cricket teams met in the Men’s Asia Cup 2025 and seemed to carry the bitterness of the conflict onto the field.
India’s players avoided shaking hands with Pakistanis, who made gestures linked to the cross-border aerial fight. The tournament ended with the victorious Indian team refusing to accept the trophy from the Pakistani head of the Asian Cricket Council.
The pattern has followed every India-Pakistan cricket encounter and even found its way into the Under-19 Asia Cup, where Indian players’ behaviour after sealing a win was heavily criticised.
Indian cricket fan Khan believes many players don’t want to partake in such aggression but are “forced into the act” at the behest of politicians and the younger generation is following suit.
“Cricket boards should take disciplinary action against [such] players and ensure that this behaviour is not passed on to the next generation.”
Khan’s teammate and good friend, Hussain, agreed.
“It is a worrying sign for the sport,” he said of the on-field antics.
“Politics has poisoned cricket and the fact that young cricketers show this behaviour is not good for the future of the game.”
A cultural experience
The venue for the tournament in Qatar is in the heart of Asian Town, a Doha suburb inhabited by migrants from South Asia who work in the capital’s Industrial Area.
For several thousand workers, a tournament bringing their home nations to their neighbourhood is a welcome change from the everyday grind of their work lives.
To have these matches a short walk away from their accommodation is an added bonus.
However, the lure of an India-Pakistan cricket match brought fans from across the Gulf state.
Doha resident Avinash Daniel, originally from India’s capital New Delhi, brought along his young family and two friends after hearing about the fixture.
“It’s our first time watching an India-Pakistan match at a stadium and it’s been a great experience,” Daniel said.
Sweeping his gaze around the stand, he pointed out that a mix of Indian and Pakistani fans surrounded his group but they were happily mingling with each other.
“There are no different sides in the stands,” he said with a shrug. “No Indian stands, no Pakistani stands. We are all mixed. It’s a wonderful cultural experience.”
Daniel, a railway engineer, believed the politicisation of cricket only benefits politicians, not cricketers or fans, who only want to enjoy the sport that offers a brief respite to its billions of fans.
“At the end of this match, both Indians and Pakistanis will go out and eat the same mandi – a traditional Arab rice and meat dish – probably cooked and served by Indians and Pakistanis.”

Ruto cut short his regional tour to travel to the Republic of Congo for high-level ta
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 23 – President William Ruto has returned to Bungoma to resume his Western Kenya tour, with sugar bonus payments to Nzoia Sugar Factory farmers taking centre stage during his visit to Webuye West.
Ruto cut short his regional tour to travel to the Republic of Congo for high-level talks with Democratic Republic of Congo President Félix Tshisekedi before returning to Kenya to continue his engagements.
Farmers expected to benefit from bonus payments as the government steps up efforts to address long-standing concerns in the industry.
The payments are particularly significant for Nzoia Sugar farmers, who have faced challenges over delayed payments, production costs and the financial difficulties affecting the sugar industry.
Ruto’s visit to Webuye West also signals that his Western Kenya tour remains on course, with the President expected to continue engaging residents and highlighting his administration’s development projects.
His return comes after Sunday’s meeting in Oyo, Republic of the Congo, where he and Tshisekedi agreed to rebuild diplomatic relations, facilitate the return of ambassadors and strengthen economic and security cooperation between the two countries.
The meeting was facilitated by Congo President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese President Faure Gnassingbé attending as the African Union-appointed mediator.

items.title: Is the global far right really in retreat?
items.summary:
Is the global far right really in retreat?
Electoral defeats alone will not dismantle the political forces that brought the far right to power.
Not too long ago, we were grappling with the surge of a global far-right alliance. And in early 2025, when United States President Donald Trump returned for
items.text:
Is the global far right really in retreat?
Electoral defeats alone will not dismantle the political forces that brought the far right to power.
Not too long ago, we were grappling with the surge of a global far-right alliance. And in early 2025, when United States President Donald Trump returned for a second term, members of this global alliance must have felt that they were on the brink of securing a global hegemony.
Yet, less than two years in, this alliance seems to be losing its grip on power – and fast.
The first casualty was Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, whose reign of 16 years ended earlier this year with a decisive loss in the parliamentary elections. He was somewhat of a “golden boy” of this movement, as Hungary under him had become the pinnacle of far-right state capture.
In fact, Orban was so important to the global right that he received election endorsements from the likes of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel. Even US Vice President JD Vance showed up in Budapest five days before the elections to reiterate the Trump administration’s endorsement of Orban’s bid for a fifth consecutive term in office.
In a tight race in late October, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva secured a fourth term after defeating far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the run-off. Notably, Lula’s challenger was the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro senior is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup following his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election.
Netanyahu has been a central figure in the global alliance of the far right. At a time of genocidal violence and pogroms targeting Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and across the occupied West Bank, Netanyahu’s far-right friends have remained unmoved in their support of Israel.
But on October 27, neither the Netanyahu-led bloc nor any opposition alliance secured the required 61 seats in the parliamentary elections. Because opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot received the endorsement of Arab-led parties, he has now been invited by President Isaac Herzog to form the next government.
In the 2026 Serbian parliamentary elections, the Student List defeated Aleksandar Vucic’s party. This was a resounding victory for the student-led anticorruption movement that took to the streets against the populist leader after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people.
Of course, the most significant challenge to the far right’s bid for global capture came in the form of the “blue wave” in the 2026 US midterm elections. On their way to victory, many Democratic candidates openly embraced progressive agendas, publicly expressed support for the Palestinian cause, criticised Israel and the role of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) in US politics and blasted their establishment predecessors for their “middle of the road” stance on issues at home and abroad.
Following a damning critique of the Trump administration, the Democratic Party is now set to control both chambers of Congress from January.
Already last year, Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York City’s mayoral election showed that a progressive candidate could overcome opposition from both the right and the Democratic establishment. His run for office was marred by xenophobic and Islamophobic attacks coming from both Republicans and establishment Democrats.
He was also accused of anti-Semitism for his criticism of Netanyahu and his past pro-Palestine organising. Yet, it was his unrelenting focus on making New York more affordable and liveable and his refusal to back down from his criticism of Israel during an ongoing genocide that gave him the win in the end.
Despite all this, I would say the demise of the far right is not yet a done deal.
Undoubtedly, far-right leaders everywhere will closely study the recent defeats of their political allies and learn from their mistakes. They will have noticed the fragility of the cult of personality of the likes of Orban in the face of years of repression and state-sanctioned corruption. They will also learn from Trump’s militarism and misadventures in the Middle East. Proclaiming a war thousands of miles away as an existential battle for the good of humanity cannot eclipse the everyday concerns of common citizens.
Most importantly, though, they will bank on the historical failings of the left. They know that without a systematic effort to remedy the conditions that led to the rise of the far right in the first place, the establishment liberals will not be able to convert these wins into long-term gains.
It is, of course, easy to attribute the global rise of the far right to the machinations of individual leaders. The Netanyahus, Bolsonaros, Modis and the Trumps of the world are undoubtedly the mascots of this movement’s global ambitions. And so it is comforting to believe that the fall of an individual leader would bring about the demise of the political movement.
But to believe this would be to ignore the fact that their rise to power is only a symptom of wider structural malaise in politics and society. These leaders have weaponised legitimate public concerns regarding youth unemployment, the hollowing of the public sector, income inequality, neoliberalisation and “big money” in politics into fodder for repression, culture wars, militarism, racism and xenophobia.
The far right may have suffered losses at the ballot box because of its misadventures in power. But if progressives are to make significant gains, it cannot be business as usual.
Concretely, in a place like the US, this means that we have to recognise that the “blue wave” was more of an assertive vote against Trump rather than a wholehearted embrace of the Democratic Party. items.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
items.summary:
Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
- Published
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
items.text:
Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
- Published
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
- Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external
- The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
- Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.
Countries divided over approach on fossil fuels
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
- Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed 
  - Published3 hours ago
Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".
While the Russian delegate, Sergei Kononuchenko, switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
COP31 had some good news
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.
On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

items.summary:

November 23, 2026

items.text:
Rule-breaking is contagious – and good examples barely help
November 23, 2026
Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?
A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.
A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."
How was the study done, and what are its limits?
The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.
Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.
Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.
The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.
Is rule-breaking contagious?
Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.
Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.
Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.
Do good role models make people follow rules?
Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.
People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.
Are people more likely to break rules when their own side does?
People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.
Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.
Can a few bad apples spoil the whole group?
To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.
In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.
What does this mean in real life?
Molleman calls the work fundamental science and says the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.
He also says it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."
This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.
