items.text:
A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.
By Jerry James ·
With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.
OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.
That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.
Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.
Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).
The short version
Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.
What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home?
Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:
- A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup.
- Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth.
- An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section.
That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.
Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run?
It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.
On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.
What Is Quantization?
Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.
The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.
If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.
Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM?
For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.
Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.
If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs.
If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.
Small
- 8-12 GB
- UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M
- 8K-16K
Medium
- 16 GB
- Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE)
- Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M
- 16K-32K
Large
- 24 GB
- UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S
- 16K-32K
Extra Large
- 32 GB+
- UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K
- 64K-128K+
Models marked MoE (mixture of experts) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way.
Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate.
Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090?
Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no.
Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context.
Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2.
2-bit
- 10-11 GB
- 12 GB card
3-bit
- 13-15 GB
- 16 GB card
4-bit (recommended)
- 17-18 GB
- 24 GB card
8-bit (lossless)
- 24 GB
- 32 GB card
Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower.
Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station, not a graphics ca

items.title: Pochettino’s new-manager bounce falls flat with De Ligt move a disastrous step | Jamie Jackson
items.summary:
Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino.
This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferg
items.text:
Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino.
This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.
He is firmly in the dock for this loss, due to a disastrous preference for Matthijs de Ligt over Harry Maguire, the hapless Dutch defender playing a leading part in three Liverpool goals.
Towards the end the Kop chirped: “You’re going down with the City.” There may be truth in the humour unless Pochettino gets hold – fast – of the rabble inherited from Michael Carrick.
Eight short minutes into a nascent tenure and a disgusted shake of his flowing locks was the greeting to the madhouse he has taken over. By then Leny Yoro had been sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak and Anfield was in bearpit mood.
Very far from ideal – and worse was to follow. Far worse. After the Frenchman departed, Dominik Szoboszlai smashed the free-kick through a nonexistent wall and beyond Senne Lammens and Liverpool were 1-0 up.
The visitors’ next act? To enter full meltdown as Diogo Dalot allowed Rio Ngumoha room to cross and Florian Wirtz hooked home, De Ligt losing his man.
Thirteen minutes in and 2–0 behind made Omar Berrada’s talk of the “buzz” of Pochettino’s entrance at United farcical and made the chief executive appear to be as much as a chump as his latest appointee, who was authoring a new head-coach plummet, not bounce.
Yoro had been forced into hauling down Isak after De Ligt lost first the ball, then the Liverpool striker. De Ligt’s inclusion was Pochettino’s headline selection move, the dropping of Maguire handing the centre-back a first league start in a year and it backfired almost immediately.
“I don’t know who played the last game – we assessed the squad from the day we arrived and we believe it’s the best team for today,” Pochettino said beforehand when quizzed about the XI he sent out.
Words to haunt him and, as De Ligt’s only other start was in United’s 4-1 humiliation at Como last month in the Champions League, questions regarding the coach’s judgment were already being posed.
By now “sacked in the morning” was the derisory cry of Kopites as Pochettino’s new project was in the damage-limitation mode of a 5-3-1 with 21 minutes played, as off went Bryan Mbeumo for Maguire.
After spells with Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USA, Pochettino’s honours roll reads one Ligue 1 and one Coupe de France – a modest two trophies in a 17-year managerial career.
Losing a Champions League final (with Spurs) and two EFL Cup finals (Spurs and Chelsea) had characterised him, to some, as a “bridesmaid” and at half‑time his team were definitively second best, fortunate to be only two behind.
In the perpetual soap opera that is United, the buildup featured a drone filming Pochettino’s first training session, Berrada’s interview and Bruno Fernandes saying new contract talks between the captain and club were paused due to the worst league start in 40 years.
Going into the game, United’s dire form contained a solitary win in 10 league matches and eight points. Why? Because they are a rabble, lacking cohesion from goalkeeper to attack, with individuals consistently embarrassing themselves and the shirt.
It cost Carrick, culpable for this too, his job and cleared the path for Pochettino to occupy a role he has long coveted. Each new manager since Ferguson has faced a two-pronged challenge: the state of the squad and the state of the club – each related.
Those who know Pochettino say he will bring charm and warmth – useful, maybe, for man-managing a group of multimillionaires, but at the interval he needed to perform the miracle of convincing them that something, somehow, could be salvaged after a diabolical opening 45 minutes.
They were staring at defeat by an Andoni Iraola side that began 10 points and 15 places better off. Pochettino hoped to avoid this by taking off Matheus Cunha for Joshua Zirkzee for the second half but ended the non-contest ashen‑faced, with Berrada and Jason Wilcox, the director of football, appearing just as lost in the posh seats.
A main takeaway from Berrada’s interview was his conviction that “we are heading in the right direction”. When he spoke United were 18th, and by full time they were 19th, with De Ligt a glaring emblem of their disarray. When again he was marking air not Isak, the Swede saved the centre-back more blushes by spraying wide.
This had Pochettino applauding, unfathomably, when invective seemed an apt response.
Yet when Ngumoha made it 3-0 after 66 minutes there was no more faux touchline enthusiasm from a man who had promised to “create something from scratch”. As with all who have followed Ferguson, he had discovered that United’s shaky foundations make building anything sustainable a sisyphean task.
De Ligt’s loose pass led to Víctor Muñoz’s fourth, meaning the answer to whether Pochettino’s debut could have gone any worse was a resounding no.

Jeeno Thitikul claimed a two-shot victory over Aki Iwai, with Nelly Korda finishing in third spot; Thitikul becomes the first player to win three consecutive CME Group Tour Championship titles and passes Annika Sorenstam in the LPGA Tour career money list
Sunday 22 November 2026 20:41, UK
Jeeno Thitikul has won the LPGA Tour's season-ending CME Group Tour Championship for a third consecutive year after storming to a two-shot victory in Florida.
Thitikul carded an eagle and five birdies during an impressive seven-under 65, pulling her clear of a congested leaderboard at Tiburon Golf Club and securing a 12th LPGA Tour title.
She finished on 24 under and two clear of Aki Iwai, who raced into contention with six birdies in the final 10 holes of her final-round 65, while world No 1 Nelly Korda finished in third spot.

items.title: Gary Neville on De Ligt selection and 'negligent' Man Utd
items.summary:
Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd: Gary Neville on Matthijs de Ligt selection and 'negligent' Red Devils
Manchester United were thrashed 4-0 by Liverpool in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as head coach after Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card; Red Devils have conceded 34 goals in all competitions this season
items.text:
Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd: Gary Neville on Matthijs de Ligt selection and 'negligent' Red Devils
Manchester United were thrashed 4-0 by Liverpool in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as head coach after Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card; Red Devils have conceded 34 goals in all competitions this season - the most by any side in Europe's major leagues
Sunday 22 November 2026 20:32, UK
Gary Neville accused Manchester United's hierarchy of negligence for failing to strengthen their defence as their 4-0 loss to Liverpool left them with the worst defensive record in Europe.
Liverpool ran riot after Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card at Anfield as goals from Dominik Szoboszlai, Florian Wirtz, Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz ensured Mauricio Pochettino suffered a horror start to his Manchester United tenure.
United have now conceded 34 goals in all competitions this term. It is the highest total of any side across Europe's top-five leagues. The result keeps them second from bottom in the Premier League.
"It's negligent," said Sky Sports pundit Neville.
- Match report | As it happened | Teams | Stats
- Live Premier League table | Watch FREE PL highlights
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW 📺
"The negligence is not bringing in defenders in the transfer window, because we've seen this for two or three years."
Pochettino made the decision to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 357 days at Anfield but the Netherlands international was partly at fault for the opening goal and endured a torrid evening along with the rest of United's defenders.
Watching back the opener, when De Ligt misjudged a high ball, Neville said: "The minute that De Ligt makes that run in that channel, Yoro has to come across within 10 metres of him, and [Diogo] Dalot has to come across. This is so bad from Yoro and Dalot.
"De Lift makes a right mess of it. He can't believe it though, De Ligt. He's played centre-half before. He can't believe Yoro's not there. Then Yoro makes contact and it's clumsy.
"Honestly. You can't get worse that that.
"You've got a back four who are looking after their own jobs, they're in fear.
"De Ligt and Martinez have dropped off, Dalot's not coming quickly enough.
"It's a mess because of the fact they've got no confidence and haven't got the ability to play out there at Anfield in a game against Liverpool."
Neville 'very surprised' by De Ligt call
Neville was baffled by Pochettino's decision to start De Ligt, who was similarly poor when returning from injury in last month's 4-1 loss to Como in the Champions League.
"We were in the trucks over in the compound and when the team came through straight away we were very surprised," added Neville.
"I just didn't think Manchester United would win, and I thought they would concede lots of goals and make mistakes.
"Maybe the options on the bench aren't brilliant either, but it's really desperate and it's tiring watching them.
"Mauricio Pochettino's options are not great, but I didn't get De Ligt.
"Having been out for a year myself, it's really difficult to come back into a game like that.
"I'm not saying that you can't, but as a centre-back getting your bearings… You saw him in Como, he was all over the place in Como.
"It's almost like you don't know what's happening. I found that coming back into it when I was 32, he's obviously more experienced as well.
"I was very surprised he played but then the others haven't been doing great either."
'That back four will get you relegated'
United's total of eight points after 11 games is their lowest at this stage of a season since the 1972/73 campaign.
"You wonder how low it can get, but this is as low as it's been in 54 years," added Neville.
"A few weeks ago against Fulham, I said it's the worst 40 minutes or 30 minutes I've seen in my lifetime.
"At the time people said that was maybe a bit too much, but this is actually the worst Manchester United have ever been in 54 years. It's a fact.
"The worst defensive team in Europe, second bottom in the league, they've never started this badly."
He added: "I would have started with Harry Maguire today. Manchester United's best back four - and I think we're informed enough to know, we've watched these lads for two or three years - is [Luke] Shaw, Dalot, Maguire and [Lisandro] Martinez.
"Now, it's a poor back four, let me be really clear. But it is Manchester United's best back four.
"Now, if you can get that back four out on the pitch, it does win games, against Liverpool last year, it does win games against City and Arsenal, it can compete slightly.
"But that back four that started today, and the one that finished against Villa a few weeks ago of [Noussair] Mazraoui, [Patrick] Dorgu, Yoro, and [Ayden] Heaven - that will get you relegated, that's a fact."

items.title: What Happened to Silicon Valley?
items.summary: On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years.
items.text:
On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above.
It’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision.
Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain.
That is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong?
The web I thought we were building in 1993
But let me start with my own history. I started my company more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill.
My original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN, the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way.
Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind.
The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for attention. Our hand-curated catalog of the best websites was soon surpassed by algorithmic solutions like those provided by Google. The amount of content produced was far larger than purely human curation could manage. It was an early example of what Richard Sutton was later to call “the bitter lesson” in his analysis of AI training.
In my 2005 essay “What Is Web 2.0?” I described how the companies that survived the dotcom bust had all, in one way or another, figured out how to help people navigate the resulting information explosion at scale. As Herbert Simon noted in 1971, an abundance of information leads to a scarcity of attention. In the face of increasing information abundance, he predicted that we would use machines to help us better allocate our time and attention. And so it has transpired: Information has become so abundant that it defies manual curation. Instead, powerful, proprietary algorithmic systems use the data they collect to match users with the answers, news, entertainment, products, applications, and services they seek. Today’s AI is in many ways a continuation of this arc.
I called this “harnessing collective intelligence.” All of it was, in economic terms, a set of remarkable advances in networked, data-enabled market coordination. It felt like a public good even when it was privately owned.
Hal Varian, formerly Google’s chief economist, once told me that only about 6% of Google search result pages carry any advertising or are otherwise monetized by Google. The other 94% were served up by search in a glorious demonstration of abundance, the surplus of value created over value captured. And while many of the pages themselves were commercial, even more were the product of the joyful exuberance of humanity, people creating and sharing for the joy of it. Google’s algorithm matched that creation to the people who wanted it, with no price involved anywhere in the transaction. Forty thousand times a second, Google’s organic search algorithms were performing the coordination that twentieth-century economists thought could only be done by self-interested actors haggling over prices. items.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
items.summary:
I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.
A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest in the smash video game series from Rocks
items.text:
I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.
A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released. 
Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy. 
But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous GTA games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however, GTA 6’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species.
I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.
(Side note: Pre-release marketing for GTA 6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)
I am one hour in and I’ve found 16/60 birds https://t.co/81x42O1BuY
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants!
After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!
Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. Looking through my binoculars I spotted my first Herring Gull—and noticed that the people, a woman and three men, were fully and visibly naked. Jason apparently lives next to a nudist resort. It’s just like being in South Florida!
Two down, 58 to go. I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets, before venturing out into the huge map. My strategy for finding birds in GTA 6 was the same as finding birds in real life: look in as many habitats as I could find. I started by “borrowing” a fanboat off a nearby dock and heading back to the swampy areas near the seaplane mission. There were tons of birds across the open water and in the marsh: Caspian Terns, Mottled Ducks, Sanderlings, Spotted Sandpipers, Great Blue Herons, Glossy and White Ibis, and … flocks of Whooping Cranes?
incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
In fact, I found a number of avian inaccuracies in just my first few hours of playtime. Certain species like Whooping Crane and Red-cockaded Woodpecker are common throughout the map, despite being endangered and threatened, respectively, in real life. Golden Eagles are extremely rare in Florida, but I found one soaring over the Mt. Kalaga area (mountains, one may point out, aren’t found in Florida either). Some species have confusing naming quirks—the chickadee is Black-capped instead of Carolina, and there’s a “New World Oriole” instead of a Baltimore Oriole—but those changes are likely due to the fact that Carolina and Baltimore don’t exist in the GTA universe.
Though some of the inaccuracies may feel like a letdown in a game that is being hailed as the Greatest of All Time, I think it’s important to remember that it’s also game where you can get a ride from a dog driving a jet ski. Grand Theft Auto games are meant to be fun, not science. Plus, despite some of the misfires, the avifauna feels well thought-out. The map is true to the ecological boundaries of South Florida, with herons, gulls, and other waterbirds in the south while birds like Red-bellied Woodpecker, Wood Stork, and American Robin are found farther north. Birders know that certain exotic species have made their home in tropical South Florida, including Spot-breasted Oriole and Red Junglefowl, both in the game.
That geographic fidelity is the main tip for anyone looking to check off all the game’s birds: Find their habitat. The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything. Wading birds, shorebirds, and seabirds are common in the southern coastal part of the map. A number of smaller, open-country or forest birds are found up north. Owls come out at night. Birds in zoos and domestic farmyard birds count towards the 60, too, so don’t overlook those areas.
Wild Boar roadkill. It’s just like birding in Florida! https://t.co/gT84IticOK
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026

items.text:
From conceding seven to Hull heroics - how Tzolakis recovered to defy Brighton
- Published
Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic used one word to describe the performance of his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis in Sunday's 2-0 Premier League win against Brighton.
"Unbelievable," he told Match of the Day.
"Especially after the international break, which was very difficult for him."
Tzolakis' previous outing had been for Greece against the Netherlands in the Uefa Nations League, where he and his side were humbled 7-0 by the hosts in Amsterdam.
Nine days later, his contribution to the Tigers' first league victory since 29 August was every bit as important as that of striker Oli McBurnie, who netted both goals in second-half stoppage time against the second-placed Seagulls.
Tzolakis made a series of top saves to keep the highest scorers in the top flight at bay and, when Brighton full-back Costinha was sent off in the 89th minute for a second bookable offence, the hosts seized their opportunity to clinch only their third win following their Premier League return.
McBurnie said the 24-year-old stopper had "kept Hull in a few games" this season and the club were "lucky to have him", while Tzolakis told Sky Sports: "We are a unit and a team.
"We play for each other. We showed a good team effort and we deserved the three points."
'Always in the right place at the right time'
With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just could not find a way past former Olympiacos goalkeeper Tzolakis, who joined Hull in August for a reported £20m fee.
He got down to make a vital block early on to deny Diego Gomez, who had slid in to meet a low cross from the left wing. It was the first of several occasions the Paraguay international would be frustrated in front of goal.
Tzolakis then raced out spreadeagled to foil Georginio Rutter with an outstretched left hand - a stop that BBC Radio 5 Live pundit and former striker Clinton Morrison described as "Peter Schmeichel-esque", referring to the legendary Denmark keeper.
Second-half efforts from distance by Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk were dealt with, too.
Yasin Ayari went close with a thumping strike against the bar and when Brighton substitute Charalampos Kostoulas pounced on a short backpass to go through one-on-one, Tzolakis got a hand on his Greece team-mate's shot and Regan Slater was back on the goalline to head the ball to safety.
Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy, a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said: "We saw again how important Tzolakis is for Hull. He had one of those days where he was always in the right place at the right time.
"When you are a Hull player and you see the kind of saves Tzolakis made when he spread himself and kept it out with his foot, you start thinking that it could be your day.
"It happens a lot in football and, on the flip side, Brighton will have been thinking, 'are we ever going to score here?'."
Hull made a superb start to the campaign after being promoted via the Championship play-offs in May.
They followed victories against Manchester United and Coventry with a draw against Aston Villa - all without conceding a goal.
The Tigers had not won since that 1-0 success at Coventry until beating Brighton - but they are one of four top-flight sides still unbeaten at home and have not lost any fixture by more than a one-goal margin.
They lost 1-0 to champions Arsenal before the international break and Scotland forward McBurnie told Match of the Day: "We know we can make it difficult for the top teams in the league and we've proved that in the past two games.
"We want to make it as difficult as we can for teams to come here and make the MKM Stadium a tough place to come. It's proving that way so far, so long may it continue."

items.title: 'No chance!' - Poch and Mainoo fume at 'unfair' Yoro red card
items.summary:
Leny Yoro red card: Man Utd boss Mauricio Pochettino and Kobbie Mainoo angry at sending off for foul on Liverpool's Alexander Isak
Manchester United were thumped 4-0 by Liverpool following Leny Yoro's red card after eight minutes; one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvi
items.text:
Leny Yoro red card: Man Utd boss Mauricio Pochettino and Kobbie Mainoo angry at sending off for foul on Liverpool's Alexander Isak
Manchester United were thumped 4-0 by Liverpool following Leny Yoro's red card after eight minutes; one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvious Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGS), is the likelihood of the attacking player "keeping or gaining control of the ball"
Sunday 22 November 2026 19:46, UK
Mauricio Pochettino felt Manchester United were given an "unfair" red card in their 4-0 defeat at Liverpool - with Kobbie Mainoo replying "no chance" when asked whether Leny Yoro should have been sent off.
Pochettino's first United game started in dismal fashion as Yoro was given his marching orders in the eighth minute for bringing down Alexander Isak as the last defender outside the box.
Dominik Szoboszlai then scored from the resulting free-kick and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead after 13 minutes. Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz put gloss on the scoreline after half-time.
- Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd - report and reaction
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- No Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW 📺
However, Yoro's sending off was doused in controversy as Isak took a heavy touch into United goalkeeper Senne Lammens before going down under the challenge.
Under the laws, one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvious Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGS), is the likelihood of the attacking player "keeping or gaining control of the ball".
Pochettino felt that not only did Isak lose control of the ball with his touch, but also that United should have been given a penalty for Jeremy Jacquet's challenge on Bryan Mbeumo at the opposite end just moments before.
"So painful. So disappointed," Pochettino told Sky Sports. "It's not ok to start a game in the Premier League with this situation.
"The game changed completely after six minutes. Now we can explain everything but the damage is done, it's so painful.
"The players are so, so feeling the pain of the result. I told them to be calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.
"We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy."
Pushed on whether he was unhappy with Isak's heavy touch, the United boss replied: "The ball was for the goalkeeper.
"In that situation, if you review the VAR you can see for sure, [Yoro] never had the intention to connect with Isak. When the control was long with the striker, the ball was going to the goalkeeper, he runs and goes down.
"In Leny's case, it wasn't intentional."
But then Pochettino added: "If you look before, on the sixth minute. Jacquet on Mbeumo. Similar? No. If you compare the actions, that was a penalty.
"How that changes life, if you score after six minutes. Now, for sure, we are talking in a different way. We have to take responsibility, I take the responsibility. We keep pushing."
Pochettino was seen speaking to the officials at full-time and when asked on that, the United boss said: "It's not going to change what happened. Being respectful is the most important.
"At the same time, I have to defend my club. And tell what I feel. That was an action that everyone who plays football, it was clear that a situation that was not a red card."
Mainoo: No chance it's a red card
United midfielder Mainoo was equally angry at the call. "The game's been taken out of our hands by a red card that I don't think can be a red card," he said.
"No chance. The ball's already with the goalkeeper. They're both running full speed. What can we do? It is what it is.
"It's 10 vs 11, you come to a place like Anfield, it's a tough game anyway. Then you lose a man, it makes it hard. I can't fault the boys for their fight in the game. We take the pain and move on.
"I wouldn't say it all goes out the window. You can still take the things you did in training into the game, but it makes it 10 times harder with one less man in a situation like that.
"It's hard, it's painful. But no one's coming to save us. We have to work hard, keep digging, keep working, keep fighting. It will all come round."
Keane: Isak is not getting the ball
There was comical defending for the Yoro red-card incident, with United defender Matthijs de Ligt - playing his first Premier League minutes of the season - letting a long ball drop that allowed Isak to run through.
That then led to the Yoro 'foul' - but Roy Keane felt it was unfair on United, even despite their poor defending.
"Isak's not getting the ball," he said. "There's no way he's getting the ball.
"It's clumsy from United. Obviously it's one straight ball over the top. You shouldn't be in so much trouble.
"But there's no way he's getting that ball. Absolutely not. I know Isak is quick and he's sharp, but we've looked at it again.
"It's really poor defending. Players not smelling danger. But Isak is not getting that ball. Absolutely not."
Pochettino defended United's defending - as they became the worst defence in Europe when it comes to goals conceded across all competitions this season.
"I wasn't in the past," said Pochettino, referring to United's defensive record under his predecessor Michael Carrick.
"I take responsibility for today, and today we concede four goals with 10 men, and in a circumstance after playing 80 minutes on Anfield with 10 men.
"Of course I take responsibility about that, no worries, but I don't want to compare situations in the past."
Pochettino defends De Ligt selection call
When put to him that United did not have to go and concede four goals after the sending off, he replied: "It's so easy to talk in this way.
"It's about the team, always it's about balance. It's not about one line, the defensive line, the midfield, the offensive. I think when the team concede it is because the balance is not so good,

items.title: Liverpool hand Pochettino nightmare Manchester United start after Yoro sees red
items.summary: Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast-furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino’s debut descended into an ordeal after merely eight minutes when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying
items.text:
Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast-furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino’s debut descended into an ordeal after merely eight minutes when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else.
Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after a comfortable, utterly dominant win peppered by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai, Victor Muñoz and the two creative forces. “Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic day in the job.
The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who only met his new charges on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake, and one that contained destructive repercussions for the entire United team and their performance.
That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia himself but his replacement at centre-half was heavily responsible for the chaos that unfolded. The Netherlands international was ultimately at fault for three goals. Liverpool, under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the mishaps in the visitors’ central defence.
De Ligt lost both the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger unfolding around his fellow centre-half. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save him. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.
A simple detail showed the extent of the job that Pochettino has on his hands: the United wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the stranded exception of Bruno Fernandes, there was no one covering the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.
Liverpool seized on the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United at Anfield did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha, starting on the left with Cody Gakpo out injured, tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.
The first chants of “Sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was of course a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.
Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead further. Lammens denied both and Maguire threw himself in the way of another Isak shot to deflect over.
Iraola must have had a word during the interval as Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from the £116m recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery from Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal that Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before rolling an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert at the back post.
Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the Champions League trip in Brugge in midweek and he made a triple substitution to rest players in the 72nd minute. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, enabled the hosts to pounce and Wirtz released Muñoz free inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do in the directors box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend, the actor James Nesbitt. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

items.text:
Yoro sees red as Ngumoha shines - Liverpool v Man Utd player ratings
- Published
Mauricio Pochettino's reign as Manchester United manager got off to a dismal start as his side were beaten 4-0 by rivals Liverpool after playing 82 minutes with 10 men.
Here's how BBC Sport rated the players - and you can see how you scored them below.
- What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? 
  - Published21 August
Liverpool
Alisson Becker: Caught one cross and took a few goal-kicks. Made a good save to deny Bruno Fernandes in stoppage time. Had little else to do. 6
Ronald Araujo: Never really tested defensively. Made a few contributions going forward. 7
Jeremy Jacquet: Went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo in the box at 0-0, although a penalty against the French defender would have been harsh. 6
Virgil van Dijk: Organised the defence well. Also had a header well-saved at 0-0 and nodded another wide in the second half. 7
Milos Kerkez: Always keen to drive Liverpool up the pitch. Had some nice link-ups with Rio Ngumoha. 7
Dominik Szoboszlai: Fantastic driven free-kick to open the scoring. Went close a few more times with long shots and generally bossed the midfield. 8
Alexis Mac Allister: Did all the simple things right and allowed others to shine around him. Forced Senne Lammens into a top save in the first half. 7
Bradley Barcola: Missed a few chances to score his first league goal for Liverpool when through one-vs-one. Showed his electric pace to set up his side's third. 7
Florian Wirtz: Readjusted well to net Liverpool's second and assisted their fourth. Five goals in four games for club and country now and looks close to his creative best. 8
Rio Ngumoha: So direct and skilful. Scored Liverpool's third with a calm finish. Also set up their second after easily beating Diogo Dalot. Club and country have a real talent on their hands. 9
Alexander Isak: Led the line well but missed some big chances. Won the free-kick that resulted in Szoboszlai's goal and led to Leny Yoro's sending off. 6
Subs:
Victor Munoz (on 72, Barcola): Good cameo and took his goal well, curling it into the far corner. 7
Trey Nyoni (on 72, Mac Allister): Looked bright. Had a shot go just over. 6
Jeremie Frimpong (on 78, Ngumoha): 5
Joe Gomez (on 85, Araujo) 5
Lewis Koumas (on 85, Isak) 5
Subs not used: Chiesa, Mamardashvili, McConell, Tsimikas.
Manchester United
Senne Lammens: Could he have done better with the opener? Good save to deny Mac Allister and some decent stops after that. 6
Leny Yoro: Did he have to make the tackle on Isak? It was almost as though he thought about whether he should and decided the answer was yes. Given Liverpool scored from the free-kick it was a bad decision. 4
Matthijs de Ligt: First Premier League start in almost 12 months in middle of a back three turned into a nightmare with the early error that led to opening goal and Yoro red card. Struggled from that moment on. 4
Lisandro Martinez: Fully extended by Liverpool's attack. The least bad of the visitors' starting defence, but that isn't saying much. Exposed completely by Barcola for Liverpool's third. 5
Diogo Dalot: Given a torrid time by Ngumoha, which prompted Pochettino to bring on Maguire. Tries hard but it's not enough. 5
Youri Tielemans: Concerns about a midfield partnership with Mainoo emerge again. Not having the sustained impact required for a player of his experience. 4
Kobbie Mainoo: Twenty-one-year-old being asked to shoulder so much responsibility in an ailing team. New midfield recruits have not helped him. 5
Bryan Mbeumo: Couple of decent bursts came to nothing, then sacrificed after Yoro red card. Received consoling pat on the head from his new boss. 5
Bruno Fernandes: Early free-kick just wide and shot straight at Alisson. Given the carnage at Old Trafford this season, no wonder contract talks on hold. Furious at free-kick given against him when he thought he was through. 5
Patrick Dorgu: Asked to do an awful lot, initially as wing-back, then further back. Lucky Barcola fluffed his lines or his failure to keep an offside line would have been exposed. 5
Matheus Cunha: Tried to keep simmering frustration in check. Not easy in a losing side with no service. Replaced at the break. 5
Subs:
Harry Maguire (on 22, Mbeumo): Couldn't have expected to be called on so soon. Went into middle of back three and immediately blocked an Isak effort to prevent a third goal. Tried hard. 5
Joshua Zirkzee (on 46, Cunha): Pre-match rumours of a rare start proved unfounded. Replaced Cunha at half-time and asked to bring a different skillset to the number nine role. More physical but not as good and lost possession too easily. 4
Mason Mount (on 65, Tielemans): Only on for a couple of minutes when attempted crossfield pass went to Liverpool player and eventually a third goal. 5
Noussair Mazraoui (on 65, Dorgu): Not really sure what he was supposed to do. Tried to push forward as United's poor control brought more pressure. 4
Andrey Santos (on 87, Mainoo): 5
Subs not used: Heaton, Amad Diallo, Heaven, Lacey.

Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd: Mauricio Pochettino endures nightmare start as Leny Yoro's early red card sparks collapse
Report and free match highlights as Manchester United are routed by Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino's first game; Leny Yoro received early red card before Liverpool ran riot; defeat keeps Man Utd in relegation zone, one point off bottom
Sunday 22 November 2026 18:30, UK
Mauricio Pochettino endured a horror start to his Manchester United tenure as his 10-man side were thrashed 4-0 by Liverpool at Anfield following Leny Yoro's early sending off.
Yoro saw red in the eighth minute when he was adjudged to have made a last-man foul on Alexander Isak, with Dominik Szoboszlai slamming home the resulting free-kick.
The decision was contentious, with Isak having seemingly lost control of the ball when he was fouled, but the double blow left the visitors in disarray and Florian Wirtz added an acrobatic second only two minutes and 46 seconds after the opener.
Liverpool fans taunted Pochettino with chants of 'you're getting sacked in the morning' following the second goal.
- As it happened | Teams | Stats
- Live Premier League table | Watch FREE PL highlights
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW 📺
The Argentine's decision to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 357 days backfired spectacularly, with the 27-year-old misjudging a high ball in the lead-up to Yoro's red card before the hosts punished more shambolic defending after the break.
Rio Ngumoha added the third when he converted Bradley Barcola's low cross following a rapid counter-attack, becoming the youngest scorer in the history of the fixture, with substitute Victor Munoz netting the fourth from a through ball by the excellent Wirtz.
The four-goal defeat showed Pochettino the size of the task ahead and kept Manchester United in the Premier League relegation zone, only a point off the bottom. They have conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's major leagues in all competitions, with 34.
The defeat was the heaviest in a Manchester United manager's first game since Lal Hilditch was beaten by the same scoreline a century ago, in 1926. It is the first time in 40 years that United have been in the bottom two at this stage of a season.
For Pochettino's counterpart Andoni Iraola, the result represents his first statement win since taking charge. Liverpool move back into fourth place, only a point behind Manchester City in third and seven points behind leaders Arsenal.
WATCH: Yoro's red and all the goals
Keane: Liverpool should have scored eight or nine
Sky Sports pundit Roy Keane said: "United were desperate. So bad.
"Gary Neville's okay with 4-0? Are you telling me they could have done better? Four-nil is not too bad with 10 men? Has anyone ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done!
"People who played for the club said 4-0 is not too bad? Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what?
"We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers. When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making?
"Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine. It's unbelievable chances they had.
"And everyone's coming off the pitch saying four is not too bad? I feel like swearing."

items.title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
items.summary:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it
items.text:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power.
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.
Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.
Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.
It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.
Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?
I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago, where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.
And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity, and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.
And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water,

Camara made his debut at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix earlier this month, following Esteban Ocon's departure ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix and reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa stepping in for that race.
He also raced alongside team-mate Ollie Bearman at the Las Vegas GP, finishing 16th, with the Brazilian now retaining his place for the remainder of the season.

The 21-year-old will feature at the Qatar GP from November 27-29 and the Abu Dhabi GP the following week, ahead of taking up a full-time seat with Haas from next season.
In a statement, Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said: "We're excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and building on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America.
"I'm delighted that Rafa's embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team.
"We now get to finish the season together, which is advantageous to us all ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get under way."
Camara leads the F2 standings by seven points over Red Bull reserve Nikola Tsolov ahead of the final two rounds of the season, although would be unable to compete in both events on the same weekend.

items.title: The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?
items.summary:
The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?
- Published
Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.
It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two
items.text:
The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?
- Published
Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.
It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two goals in quick succession.
Should it have been a red card though?
Was there a case for the video assistant referee (VAR) to suggest it should be downgraded to a yellow?
Let's take a look at the incident, and what a referee takes into account before showing a red for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.
What happened and what will the officials have taken into consideration?
1 of 5
Ronald Araujo played a long ball upfield for Alexander Isak to run on to.
Isak took a touch, before Yoro bundled into the back of the Sweden international and brought him down.
Referee Sam Barrott did not hesitate, giving the foul and sending off Yoro.
Was there doubt that Isak would have taken control of the ball? If so, it should only be a caution.
There are four key considerations for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity:
- distance between the offence and the goal
- general direction of play
- likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball
- location and number of defenders and attackers
As Isak was running directly towards goal in a central position, and there was no covering defender, three of the factors were satisfied.
The question is about the "likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball".
The Liverpool striker took a heavy touch, which moved the ball a few yards ahead of him.
The touch came before contact from Yoro, so there is no case that the challenge caused Isak to over-run the ball.
The referee and the VAR, John Brooks, must therefore assess whether Isak would definitely have got to the ball ahead of Senne Lammens. And that if he had, it would have been a good scoring chance.
If there is any doubt, then it should not be a red card.
It is a borderline case, and as such the VAR would not be expected to intervene for a clear and obvious error.
Likewise, if the referee had shown a yellow the VAR would not get involved.
Former Liverpool and England midfielder Danny Murphy, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said there was "no doubt" about the red card.
Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville also agreed with the decision.
"Leny Yoro has to cover and he doesn't," Neville said on Sky Sports. "He reacts late and his anticipation is poor.
"It's so clumsy from Yoro. It's naivety, he just needs to get off the pitch. You're not going to get that turned around, no chance."
Have there been any similar incidents?
There have been a couple of very similar cases this season.
Brighton's Pascal Struijk was sent off at Sunderland through a VAR review after he brought down Wilson Isidor.
The Seagulls successfully appealed against that red card on the grounds that there was clear doubt that Isidor would have taken control of the ball before it ran through to goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.
Sounds quite similar.
Could Manchester United appeal against Yoro's red card? There's nothing to lose by doing so.
Despite the Football Association regulatory commission unanimously ruling the Struijk red card was wrong, the Premier League's key match incidents panel voted the VAR intervention was a correct call on a split 3-2 vote.
Ipswich's Issa Diop avoided a VAR red card for a foul on James McAtee against Nottingham Forest, when the referee disagreed with the video official, and believed there was a covering defender. Forest boss Oliver Glasner was adamant it had been a clear goalscoring opportunity.
It was the same referee, Thomas Bramall, for both of those incidents.
That shows just how subjective such decisions can be. It is often rare to get a real consensus.
Yoro can count himself a little unfortunate to get the red card.

Luke Littler values legacy and darts titles over money as he launches initiative to help reduce youth unemployment
Luke Littler and The Kings Trust join forces to help young people find employment through practical job skills and work experience; Littler to defend World Darts Championship title live on Sky Sports from December 11 after second-round exit at Grand Slam of Darts
Sunday 22 November 2026 18:03, UK
Luke Littler says "titles and legacy" are more important to him than money after joining forces with a youth unemployment charity to help those in his native north west of England.
Two-time world champion Littler, 19, and The Kings Trust have established the 'Luke Littler Opportunity Fund', which aims to assist young people in finding employment through practical job skills and work experience.
The world No 1, who will look for a hat-trick of titles at Alexandra Palace live on Sky Sports from December 11, told the Big Issue after becoming its youngest guest editor: "I just love what I do. Once that love for the game goes, then I'll obviously stop, whenever that is.
- World Championship now Luke Littler's 'incentive'
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream conttact-free
- Darts calendar 2026: Tournaments and winners
"It's just the drive, the momentum you get when I'm going on stage, knowing that if I hit this double, you're into the final or I'm world champion.
"Many people are like, 'oh, money's got to his head', but it's never been about the money. I've never grown up with a lot of money, so now I've got it, I'm not going to go and use it all.
"I want titles and legacy in the game of darts."
'Not everyone gets the start I had'
On his new initiative to help reduce youth unemployment, Littler, who has become an ambassador for The King's Trust, added: "Help is needed all across the country. I'd like to focus on the north because I've seen many people struggling.
"The King's Trust gives opportunities to people, whether it's to build a bit of confidence or to find their feet and find a job.
"I just want to get out there, be an ambassador and help people out. Darts has given me a path in life and opened up so many amazing opportunities for me at a young age.
"Not everyone gets the same start and I want this fund to be something we can build over the coming years and hopefully get lots of people behind it so we can make a real difference to young people across the north west."
Littler's friends also contributed to the Big Issue, including Manchester United and England footballer Ella Toone and fellow darts player Beau Greaves.
Littler said: "I've really enjoyed guest editing and getting some familiar faces involved to share their own stories.
"Hopefully, together we can get more people talking about the importance of giving young people opportunities, whatever their background."

items.text:
The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.
Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
Creator Edmund McMillen claims he ‘had no idea’ AI music was used in the latest version of Binding of Isaac.
Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.
Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

items.text:
'Rolls-Royce' Iqbal's 'dream' journey from Old Trafford to Tannadice
- Published
Given the superlatives being thrown in the direction of Zidane Iqbal by the Scottish football fraternity, one would think he was a replica of a certain France great instead of just sharing his name.
So much so that BBC Radio Scotland pundits were suggesting on Saturday's Sportsound that the 23-year-old is the answer to Celtic's hunt for a long-term successor to captain Callum McGregor as their midfield general.
It is just as well for Dundee United that the Iraq international is tied to them until at least the summer, his early season appearances for Utrecht ruling out a transfer during the January window.
So, where has he sprung from and what is all the fuss about?
- 'Goodwin due a lot of credit and kudos' 
  - Published3 hours ago
- Hibs 0-4 Dundee United: What Goodwin said 
  - Published1 day ago
Midfielder inspiring United 'masterclass'
Born in Manchester to a Pakistani father and an Iraqi mother, Iqbal came through the Old Trafford youth system.
He signed his first professional contract with United in 2021 and became the first British-born South Asian and first-ever British South Asian to play in the Champions League when he came on as an 89th-minute substitute against Young Boys that December.
However, that was to be his one and only first-team appearance and, although he had already made his international debut in a World Cup qualifier at the age of 19, he was sold to Utrecht for a reported fee of £1m in summer 2023.
Starting off in their Jong Utrecht second string, he would go on to make 49 appearances for the Dutch top-flight outfit before making a surprise switch to the Scottish Premiership this summer.
On the one hand, United were getting a player who played all three of Iraq's games at this summer's World Cup, two of them starts, albeit all three were heavy defeats.
On the other hand, Iqbal had only managed seven appearances last season for Utrecht and had been a second-half substitute in two of their four matches at the start of the new campaign.
However, after a pivotal display in what was being described as a midfield "masterclass" by United in Saturday's 4-0 dismantling of hosts Hibernian, manager Jim Goodwin revealed he always had belief the Tangerines were unearthing a "Rolls-Royce".
"The head of recruitment's job is to go and identify good talent for us," Goodwin told BBC Scotland. "It's my job to give him the profile and then he goes out and does the groundwork.
"We could see immediately when we watched the footage of Zidane and when we had the Zoom call with him and his representatives, we not only had a fantastic player but a really good person with the right characteristics to come and fit the culture here."
'Enjoy him while you can, United fans'
While on-loan Rangers man Lyall Cameron was among the goals and fellow 24-year-old Dylan Tait provided a stylish assist, it was the third leg of what some regard as the best midfield triumvirate in the Premiership who was singled out for most praise at Easter Road.
With former Celtic winger Aidan McGeady again pondering the question about McGregor's likely successor, transfer market expert and former United wing-back Allan Preston opined: "A six for Celtic? Look no further than young Iqbal.
"He's been magnificent since he's come to Scottish football, absolutely brilliant. Running the show again.
"If Celtic are looking for a young boy at his age with experience, he is a full international, knows the game, played in Scotland, you can see what he can do, there's your man in front of you.
"Other players' hair's on fire, but he's just nice and calm. He's at a different level. He doesn't panic. When the ball comes to him, he is so calm on it, he takes his time, he's got great peripheral vision."
The former Dundee United wing-back pointed out, though: "He's had his two clubs that he can play for in a year of football, so he is going nowhere until at least the summer, so enjoy him while you can because I think you'll get serious money for this young boy."
McGeady pointed to Iqbal's "good pedigree", having started with Manchester United and already having 32 caps for Iraq, but wondered if that would be enough for Celtic to consider him.
"I don't even think, if he's performing this well, Celtic will go and get him," said McGeady.
"Why are Celtic not looking at players like this? Do they feel they have to prove themselves somewhere else first?"
Former Celtic captain Scott Brown was similarly impressed.
"He's been a delight to watch - sharpness to get on the ball and willingness to drive forward," the former midfielder and manager pointed out.
"He beats a man in the middle of the park as well and there's not too many midfielders willing to do that.
"Watching him there talking to the media, he can't get the smile off his face. He enjoys football, he takes the ball under pressure, he does things that other people don't do, especially in midfield.
"He brings composure, but he can also drive through as well. His willingness to keep getting on the ball, even if he makes that slight mistake - that's what I really enjoy watching about him."
Drive from Netherlands to Scotland 'worth it'
While Goodwin reckons there will be likely interest in the summer, Iqbal has no thoughts of so quickly leaving a club - and manager - who have resurrected his club career.
"I'm not even looking at any other clubs," he told BBC Scotland. "I'm fully focused on Dundee United.
"They've given me a platform to enjoy myself and play football. I'm really enjoying my football again.
"They've given me faith and confidence. The gaffer and the coaching staff have a lot of belief in me.
"The bare minimum I can do is pay them back with strong performances and hopefully it carries on."
Iqbal recalled being at Manchester United's "development centre since I was four or five - I signed when I was eight", explaining that he "then left for some first-team football".
